chunks.title: The palace you are looking at is the fourth one
chunks.body: Look up. What you see is not the old palace. It is the fourth building on this ground. The first was wood, inside a fort, put up by the Wadiyars in the fourteenth century. Wood burns. In 1897 the palace caught fire during a royal wedding and most of it went. The regent queen decided not to patch it. She sent for a British architect, Henry Irwin, and told him to build in stone. Work ran from 1897 to 1912. So when people say this palace is six hundred years old, they are talking about the site, not the walls. The walls in front of you are about a hundred and fourteen years old.
chunks.source_name: Re-Thinking The Future, Mysore Palace by Henry Irwin

chunks.title: Who built it, and what it cost
chunks.body: The palace has a formal name: Amba Vilas. Henry Irwin designed it. He was a British architect who had already worked on public buildings in Madras and Simla. The commission came from Maharani Kempananjammanni, regent for the young Krishnaraja Wadiyar the Fourth. The style is called Indo-Saracenic. That is a mix: domes and arches from Mughal building, columns and proportions from European building, and detail from Hindu temple carving. Records put the cost at about forty-one lakh rupees, finished in 1912. Keep that number in mind as you walk. It bought grey granite, pink marble domes, stained glass shipped from Glasgow, and cast iron pillars.
chunks.source_name: Maps of India, The Royal History of Mysore Palace

chunks.title: Stand under the Kalyana Mantapa dome
chunks.body: Walk into the octagonal wedding hall and stop. Now look straight up. The ceiling is stained glass in peacock patterns, held in a cast iron frame. The frame was made in Glasgow and shipped out in pieces. Below your feet the floor is laid in small tiles, and the pattern in the floor answers the pattern in the glass. Stand in the centre and turn slowly. The light changes colour as it comes down. Late morning is when the colours are strongest, because the sun is high enough to come through the dome rather than the side windows. Give it a full minute before you move on.

chunks.title: The Dasara procession painted on the wall
chunks.body: In the long corridor there is a set of oil paintings that show the Dasara procession as it looked in the 1930s. Walk along them slowly. You are looking at a crowd portrait. The artists painted real people, and many of them are recognisable to families in this city even now. Follow the line of elephants. The one carrying the golden howdah is the point of the whole thing. In those days the Maharaja rode in it. Since 1971 the howdah carries the idol of Chamundeshwari instead. The route in the painting is still the route the procession takes today.

chunks.title: Sunday night, ninety-seven thousand bulbs
chunks.body: On Sunday evenings and public holidays the whole outside of the palace is lit with bulbs outlining every arch, dome and edge. The lighting usually runs about seven to a quarter to eight in the evening. It is worth planning your day around. Stand well back, near the Jayamarthanda gate, so you can take in the full width. The switch-on is sudden. There is a noise from the crowd when it happens. If you are here on a Sunday, do the inside of the palace in the afternoon and keep the evening free rather than trying to do both at once.

chunks.title: Shoes off, camera in the locker
chunks.body: Two things catch people out here. You leave your shoes at a counter before you go inside, so wear something you can slip off, and expect the stone to be hot in the afternoon. Cameras are not allowed inside the palace rooms. There is a camera counter just past the entry gate where you hand yours in. You can photograph the outside and the grounds freely. Opening hours are usually ten in the morning to half past five, every day. Allow ninety minutes for the inside if the queue is short, longer on a weekend.

chunks.title: The twelve temples inside the walls
chunks.body: The palace grounds hold twelve temples. Some are older than any part of the building you came to see. That is not decoration. When the Wadiyars built a fort here, the temples were already the reason the place mattered. The oldest go back to the fourteenth century. Walk the perimeter of the grounds instead of going straight to the gate, and you will pass several of them. The Shweta Varahaswamy temple near the south gate is the easiest to spot. People from the neighbourhood still come to these for ordinary daily worship. It is a working part of the city, not an exhibit.
chunks.source_name: Re-Thinking The Future, Mysore Palace by Henry Irwin

chunks.title: The double-headed bird over the gate
chunks.body: Look at the arch above the main gate. There is a bird with two heads on it. That is the Gandaberunda, the emblem of the Mysore kings. In the old stories it is a form Vishnu took to absorb the force of another god who had gone too far. Two heads, one body, enough power to hold something no single creature could hold. You will start seeing it everywhere once you have noticed it: on the palace, on state buses, on the emblem of Karnataka. The Wadiyars used it for centuries. So does the state government today.

chunks.title: Why the palace faces the hill
chunks.body: Stand at the front of the palace and look east. That hill with the temple on top is Chamundi. The palace faces it directly, and that is deliberate. Chamundeshwari is the family goddess of the Wadiyars. The city takes its name from a demon she killed. So the arrangement is simple: the ruling house built its home looking at the goddess who protects it. On a clear morning you can pick out the temple tower from here. During Dasara the two places work as one event, the hill in the day and the palace at night.

chunks.title: Eat before the palace, not after
chunks.body: There is no good food inside the palace grounds, and the stalls outside the gates are middling. Do this instead. Eat a plate of dosa at a proper place in the morning, then come here. Mylari on the Nazarbad side does a soft, ghee-heavy dosa and shuts by late morning. If you are running later, Hotel RRR near Gandhi Square opens around half eleven and does a full Andhra meal on a banana leaf. Both are ten minutes from the palace gate. Coming out of the palace hungry at three in the afternoon is a common mistake here.

chunks.title: The city is named after the one who lost
chunks.body: Here is something odd about this place. Mysuru is named after a buffalo demon called Mahishasura. Not after the goddess who killed him. The old name is Mahishuru, the town of Mahisha. He held this land and no god could put him down, so the gods pooled their strength and made Chamundeshwari. She fought him on this hill and won. The city then kept his name. You will see his statue near the top of the hill, painted, holding a sword and a snake. Most cities are named for a victor. This one is named for the one who lost.
chunks.source_name: Devi Mahatmya and local tradition, general reference

chunks.title: What the tower is telling you
chunks.body: Look at the gopura over the entrance. It is seven storeys of figures, gold-topped, and it was added in the eighteenth century by Krishnaraja Wadiyar the Third. The shrine underneath is much older, going back to Hoysala times. That is the usual pattern in south India. The holy part is small and old and dark. The tall gaudy part is a later gift from a king who wanted his name attached. Both are honest. Read the tower from the bottom up and you are reading a list of gods in order of rank, with the smaller attendants at the top.

chunks.title: Turn around at the top and look west
chunks.body: Before you join the queue, walk to the edge of the terrace and look back the way you came. The whole city is laid out below. Find the palace first, it is the big pale rectangle near the centre. Then trace the ring of lakes: Karanji to the near side, Kukkarahalli further out. On a clear morning you can see as far as the Chamundi foothills folding into farmland. In the afternoon the haze usually takes the far edge away. Early is better for this view, and early is also when the queue is shortest.

chunks.title: The queue, and how to shorten it
chunks.body: There are two ways in: the free line and the paid quick line. On an ordinary weekday morning the free line moves in twenty minutes or so. On Fridays, on Tuesdays, and through the Dasara period it can be over an hour. Ask at the counter which line is which before you commit, because the entrances are not obvious from outside. Phones are usually not allowed in the inner shrine and there are lockers near the entrance. Footwear comes off well before the door. The stone gets very hot between noon and three, so socks are worth having.

chunks.title: Dasara begins on this hill
chunks.body: For ten days in autumn this hill is the start of the whole festival. The goddess is worshipped here first, and only then does the city below light up. The procession that everyone photographs, the elephants and the golden howdah, is the closing act on the tenth day. Before 1971 the Maharaja rode in that howdah. Now the idol of Chamundeshwari rides in it and the family walks behind. The change happened when the royal titles ended. The ritual did not stop. It transferred from the king to the goddess he served.

chunks.title: Carved out of the hill it sits on
chunks.body: This Nandi was not carried up here. It was cut out of a boulder that was already on this slope. Fifteen feet high, about twenty-four feet long, one piece of granite. The date is 1659, under Dodda Devaraja Wodeyar. Walk around the back and you can still see where the rock meets the ground without a join. Look at the bell collar and the chains around the neck. Those chains are carved, not hung. Someone stood on this hillside for years taking granite away with a chisel until a bull was left behind.
chunks.source_name: Exotic India Art, Who Built the Nandi Statue

chunks.title: The oil, and why the stone is black
chunks.body: Put your hand near the stone, not on it. It looks wet. That is oil. People have been rubbing this Nandi with oil and charcoal for centuries, and the granite has drunk it. That is why a grey rock reads black. Look at the shoulders and the top of the head, where hands reach easily. Those are the darkest and the smoothest. The parts nobody can reach are still rough and grey. You are looking at three hundred and sixty years of touch, mapped onto a stone surface. Do not add to it. The oil is doing slow damage.

chunks.title: The steps are not a shortcut
chunks.body: There are around a thousand steps from the foot of the hill to the temple. People climb them barefoot as an offering. Be clear about what this is. It takes a fit person an hour going up, longer coming down, and the stone is uneven and hot after ten in the morning. If anyone in the party has bad knees or a heart condition, take the road. The bus and taxi road goes all the way to the top and the Nandi is at step number seven hundred, so you can drive up and walk down to it in ten minutes.

chunks.title: Start before six if you are climbing
chunks.body: If you are doing the steps, leave the bottom before six in the morning. Two reasons. The stone is cool, and the light comes up sideways across the city while you climb. There are small shrines cut into the rock on the way and people stop at each one, so you will not be alone even at that hour. Carry water. There are stalls but they are spaced out. At the top there is tea and there are coconuts. Coming down the same way is harder on the knees than going up, which surprises people every time.

chunks.title: A woman cursed this dynasty and the sand came
chunks.body: In 1610 a widow named Alamelamma held jewels that belonged to the temple at Srirangapatna. Raja Wadiyar wanted them. His men came for her. She went to the bank of the Kaveri at Talakad and said three things before she jumped in. Let Talakad turn to sand. Let Malangi become a whirlpool. Let the kings of Mysore never bear sons. Talakad today is buried under dunes. There is a whirlpool in the river at Malangi. And the Wadiyar line has adopted heirs again and again over four centuries. Three facts and a curse. Whether one caused the others is not something this story can tell you.

chunks.title: The adoption record, without the curse
chunks.body: Set the curse aside and look at the record. The Wadiyar succession has repeatedly gone sideways rather than straight down. Krishnaraja Wadiyar the Third had no surviving son and adopted. Chamaraja Wadiyar the Tenth came to the throne by adoption. Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar, the last ruling maharaja, had a son, but the line after him passed by adoption again in 2015. That much is documented. Sand did cover Talakad, and geologists put it down to the river shifting course and wind moving dune fields. Two true things sitting next to each other is not the same as one causing the other. The family itself has treated the curse seriously, which is also a fact.

chunks.title: The golden idol the king made afterwards
chunks.body: The story does not end at the river. Raja Wadiyar, who had sent the men, had a golden image made of Alamelamma and placed it in the palace. It is brought out and worshipped during Dasara. Think about what that means. A ruling house that took a woman's jewels and drove her to the water then installed her as a figure to be honoured, and kept doing it for four hundred years. Guilt is one reading. Insurance is another. In 2015 the family spoke publicly of building a temple for her at Talakad. The account is still open.

chunks.title: A sweet invented because a king was bored
chunks.body: Mysore pak was made in the palace kitchen. The Maharaja, Mummadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar, was tired of what the cooks were sending up and asked for something new. A cook called Kakasura Madappa took gram flour, ghee and sugar syrup, cooked it hard, poured it out and cut it. The king liked it and asked what it was called. Madappa had not named it, so he said Mysore pak on the spot. Pak means the syrup. His descendants still make it, in a small shop on Sayyaji Rao Road by the Devaraja Market building. Same family, same recipe, coal-fired pans.

chunks.title: Ask for the soft one
chunks.body: There are two kinds sold under the same name. The hard, dry, porous slab you get in most sweet shops, and the soft one that collapses when you press it. Guru Sweet Mart makes the soft kind. Ask for ghee Mysore pak. It comes warm if you get there after a fresh batch, and it will leave your fingers greasy, which is the point. Eat it the same day. It does not keep well once the ghee sets. The shop is small and there is usually a crowd at the counter, so decide what you want before you get to the front.

chunks.title: Follow your nose to the flower rows
chunks.body: Go in through the Sayyaji Rao Road side and keep walking until the smell changes. First it is vegetables, damp and green. Then it turns sharp with limes and chillies. Then it goes sweet, and you are in the flower section. Mysore mallige, the local jasmine, is sold by length, not by weight. The women measure it against their forearm. Buy a mozham, about a forearm's length. It costs very little and the scent will fill a car. Buy it in the evening. Jasmine opens after dark and the smell doubles.

chunks.title: The jasmine has a legal identity
chunks.body: Mysore mallige is not a loose description. It carries a Geographical Indication tag, which means the name is protected in law and can only be used for jasmine grown in this region. The flower is smaller than the jasmine you see elsewhere and the scent is heavier. Growers around Srirangapatna and Nanjangud supply this market before dawn. What you buy at ten in the morning was picked in the dark. That is why the sellers are impatient by afternoon: the stock has been open for hours and the scent is going.

chunks.title: Sandalwood, and how not to be fooled
chunks.body: You will be offered sandalwood here: oil, soap, small carved pieces. Real sandalwood is expensive and the trade is controlled by the state, because the trees were a royal monopoly for centuries and are still protected. Anything sold cheap in a market stall is scented wood, not sandalwood. That is not always a swindle, just be clear what you are paying for. If you want the real thing, the government emporium sells it with paperwork. What is worth buying here instead is agarbatti. Mysuru has made incense for a long time and the local sticks are good and honest.

chunks.title: The pyramids of colour by the entrance
chunks.body: Near the entrance there are cones of powder stacked into neat pyramids: vermilion, turmeric, deep pink, indigo. Those are kumkuma and rangoli powders. They are there to be bought by the spoon, not photographed, though everyone photographs them. Ask before you take a picture and most sellers will say yes and then rebuild a cone for you. The building itself is from 1886 and has been under threat of demolition more than once. Parts of the roof have fallen. Walk the outer corridor to see the old iron columns still holding it up.

chunks.title: The dosa here is not crisp, and that is correct
chunks.body: If you have eaten dosa elsewhere you are expecting something thin and brittle. This is not that. The Mysuru dosa at Mylari is thick, soft, pale and heavy with ghee. It folds rather than cracks. It comes with a white coconut chutney and no sambar, and you eat it with your hand. Order two to start. They are smaller than they look. The shop is plain, the seating is tight, and they stop when the batter runs out, usually late morning. Do not go at eleven expecting to be fed.

chunks.title: A banana leaf meal, and the order it arrives in
chunks.body: At RRR you sit and a leaf goes down in front of you. Sprinkle water on it and wipe it with your hand. Then things start arriving without being asked for: rice, a ladle of ghee, sambar, rasam, two or three vegetable sides, a fried item, curd. This is an Andhra-style meal in a Karnataka city, so expect more chilli than the local standard. Rice comes back as often as you let it. Say no with your hand over the leaf. At the end fold the leaf towards you, which means you were fed well.

chunks.title: A German cathedral in a Kannada city
chunks.body: The twin spires are one hundred and seventy-five feet high and the design is copied from Cologne Cathedral in Germany. The foundation stone was laid in 1933 by the Maharaja, Krishnaraja Wadiyar the Fourth, for a Catholic congregation in a Hindu kingdom. That is worth sitting with for a moment. Go down into the crypt below the main altar. There is a relic of Saint Philomena there, a third-century martyr. The building is Neo-Gothic: pointed arches, ribbed vaults, tall thin windows built to pull your eye upward. It works. Stand at the back, in the centre aisle, and look straight ahead.
chunks.source_name: Mysuru diocese and city records, general reference

chunks.title: Sit at the back for ten minutes
chunks.body: Come in and sit at the rear rather than walking straight up the aisle. The stained glass runs down both sides and the scenes are the standard sequence: birth, teaching, crucifixion, resurrection. In the late afternoon the light comes through the west windows and lays coloured shapes across the floor and the pews. It moves while you watch. The building is usually quiet outside Mass times and the ceiling is high enough that sound carries oddly, so voices from the far end reach you clearly. It is one of the few places in central Mysuru where you can be still.

chunks.title: The palace they lived in while the other one burned
chunks.body: This building came first. It went up in 1861, and when the main palace burned in 1897 the royal family moved here and stayed until 1912. So for fifteen years this was the palace of Mysore. Later it was turned into an art gallery. The three-tiered facade at the front was added in 1900 for a royal ceremony. Look at it before you go in. Each tier has a different rhythm of arches, and the whole front is a screen rather than a wall. Inside, the rooms are the original domestic rooms, which is why the gallery has an odd, cramped charm.
chunks.source_name: Mysuru city heritage records, general reference

chunks.title: Find the Raja Ravi Varma room
chunks.body: Go looking for the Raja Ravi Varma paintings. He was the painter who put Hindu gods into oil on canvas in a European style, and he did it in the late nineteenth century when nobody else was. Once you have seen his Lakshmi or his Saraswati you will recognise the images everywhere in India, on calendars, on packaging, on shop walls. This is where a set of the originals hangs. Stand close enough to see the brushwork on the fabric. He was very good at cloth. Then step back six feet and see why the images travelled.

chunks.title: Look for the grain of rice
chunks.body: There is a case in this gallery holding a single grain of rice with verses written on it. There is also a French musical clock where small figures come out and strike the hour, and a painting made of glass beads. The collection is unusual because it was a royal household collection rather than a curated museum, so a great painting sits next to a curiosity a maharaja happened to like. Do not skip the upper floors. The lighting is poor and the labels are old, but the odd things are worth the stairs. Allow forty minutes.

chunks.title: The dam came first, the garden was the apology
chunks.body: The Krishna Raja Sagara dam was built between 1911 and 1932 across the Kaveri, engineered by M. Visvesvaraya. It was one of the largest dams in Asia at the time and it was built with a mix of surki mortar rather than modern cement. The garden below it came afterwards, laid out in the 1920s in a formal terraced style. So the order matters: this is an engineering project with a park attached, not a park with a dam behind it. Look at the dam wall first. Then walk down into the terraces.

chunks.title: Stay for the fountains, skip the middle of the day
chunks.body: The reason to come here is the musical fountain in the evening. It runs after dark, usually around seven, and lasts about twenty minutes. Before that the garden is a garden: symmetrical beds, water channels, a lot of families. Coming at two in the afternoon in April is a mistake, there is little shade on the terraces. Come at five, walk the terraces while the light drops, cross to the far side for the fountain. The drive back to Mysuru takes about forty-five minutes and the road is busy after the show ends.

chunks.title: The islands were an accident of a dam
chunks.body: These islets formed after a small dam was built across the Kaveri here in the 1600s. Birds started nesting on them. In the 1940s the ornithologist Salim Ali walked this stretch, saw what was happening, and persuaded the Mysore government to protect it. It became a sanctuary in 1940. So the habitat is man-made and the protection came from one person noticing. Take the boat. Painted storks, spot-billed pelicans, open-billed storks, river terns. And mugger crocodiles on the rocks, close enough that the boatman will tell you to keep your hands inside.
chunks.source_name: Karnataka Forest Department records, general reference

chunks.title: Go early and take the first boat
chunks.body: The birds are active at first light and again in the late afternoon. Between eleven and three there is much less happening and the sun on the water is hard. Boats are shared and go when full, or you can pay for a private one, which is worth it if you have a camera. The nesting season runs roughly June to November and that is when the trees on the islands are loud and crowded. Outside that window it is quieter. Wear a hat. There is no shade on the boat and the trip lasts about half an hour.

chunks.title: The island where an empire changed hands
chunks.body: You are standing on an island in the Kaveri. On the fourth of May 1799 the British army broke through this wall and by evening Tipu Sultan was dead. That single day handed south India to the East India Company. Before it, Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu had fought the British four times over thirty years and twice won. After it, no Indian power south of the Krishna could resist them. Walk the breach. It is still there, on the north-west face, where the river ran shallow in May and the wall had been weakened by artillery.
chunks.source_name: V&A Museum, Tippoo's Tiger object history

chunks.title: The spot where they found the body
chunks.body: There is a marked place near the water gate where Tipu's body was found under a pile of dead men and horses. He had been fighting on foot. The British officers who found him described him as still warm. Stand at the gate and look at the passage. It is narrow, it slopes, and it was crowded with retreating soldiers when the assault came through. Nothing here is grand. It is a low stone tunnel with a plaque. That is more honest than a monument would be. Read the plaque, then walk back out and look at the wall thickness.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India site marker

chunks.title: Why the river did not save the fort
chunks.body: The Kaveri wraps around this island, which should make it hard to take. It did, twice. The difference in 1799 was timing. The British attacked in May, at the end of the dry season, when the river was at its lowest and could be waded. They had also spent weeks bombarding one section of wall from across the water. Tipu knew the weak point and was told to strengthen it. The work was not finished. Look at where the ground falls towards the river on the western side and you can see the whole plan of the assault in the landscape.

chunks.poi: Daria Daulat Bagh (Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace), Srirangapatna
chunks.title: A summer palace made of teak, not stone
chunks.body: This building is wood. Teak pillars, teak walls, a wide verandah on all four sides, set in a formal garden. It was finished in 1784. Tipu used it in summer. The British kept it after 1799 and Arthur Wellesley, later the Duke of Wellington, lived here for a while. That is why it survived when so much else on the island did not. Take your shoes off and walk the verandah first, all the way round, before you go in. The proportions only make sense once you have felt how deep the shade is.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Daria Daulat Bagh

chunks.poi: Daria Daulat Bagh (Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace), Srirangapatna
chunks.title: The wall where Tipu's army is winning
chunks.body: On the west wall of the verandah there is a mural of the battle of Pollilur, 1780. Hyder Ali's forces are destroying a British column. Look for the British officers biting their moustaches, which was the painter's way of showing dismay. Colonel Baillie is in a palanquin. The whole wall is a victory painting, and it was still on the wall when the British took the building nineteen years later. They did not scrub it off. Walk the length of it slowly. It is painted in registers, so read it like a strip, left to right.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Daria Daulat Bagh

chunks.poi: Daria Daulat Bagh (Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace), Srirangapatna
chunks.title: No photographs inside, and why the light is dim
chunks.body: Photography is not allowed inside the building. That is not fussiness. These are painted plaster surfaces, they have been repainted and restored more than once, and light is what is killing them. The interior is deliberately kept dark for the same reason. Give your eyes a minute after you step in from the garden. The small museum upstairs holds prints, coins and Tipu's belongings, including copies of the letters. Allow forty-five minutes. It is usually open through the middle of the day when other sites on the island close. Bags are checked at the door.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India site rules

chunks.title: The tiger that ate a man, by clockwork
chunks.body: Tipu Sultan called himself the Tiger of Mysore and meant it. His soldiers wore tiger stripes. His guns had tiger mouths. And in the music room of his palace on this island he kept a life-sized wooden tiger crouched over a European soldier. Turn the handle and an organ inside the tiger growled while the man's arm lifted and dropped and a pipe made a wailing sound. The British found it in 1799. Lord Wellesley shipped it to London in 1800. It is in the Victoria and Albert Museum now, object number 2545, and you can go and turn the handle no longer, but you can see it.

chunks.title: Rockets before the British had them
chunks.body: Tipu's army used iron-cased rockets. Not fireworks. Tubes of soft hammered iron packed with powder, strapped to a bamboo shaft, fired in volleys at ranges over a kilometre. They were used against the British at Pollilur and again at Srirangapatna. After 1799 the British collected the wreckage and took it home, and William Congreve worked from it to develop the Congreve rocket, which the Royal Navy then used. The line runs from this island to the rockets in the American national anthem. Some of the recovered casings are in the Royal Artillery collection in England.
chunks.source_name: Royal Artillery Museum collection, general reference

chunks.title: Three graves under one dome
chunks.body: Under this dome are three graves. Hyder Ali, who took the throne of Mysore by force. Fakhr-un-Nisa, his wife. And Tipu, their son, buried here the day after he was killed. Tipu built the tomb for his parents. He did not expect to be in it. The British buried him with military honours, in the rain, and contemporary accounts say a storm broke that evening. Walk in and let your eyes adjust. The graves are low and plain. The tiger stripes are on the doors and the walls, not on the stones.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Gumbaz Srirangapatna

chunks.title: The doors Lord Dalhousie sent
chunks.body: Look at the ebony doors inlaid with ivory. Those were a gift from Lord Dalhousie, a British Governor-General, decades after the British killed the man buried inside. The building itself is dark granite with a whitewashed dome, ringed by a corridor of polished black pillars. Walk the corridor and look at the tiger-stripe pattern painted on the interior walls. It is called babri, and it was Tipu's personal device. The garden outside is a formal Mughal-style char bagh with cypresses. Go early. The pillars take the morning light well and the crowd builds by ten.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Gumbaz Srirangapatna

chunks.title: The temple is older than everything around it
chunks.body: This temple has been here since the ninth century, long before Tipu, long before the Wadiyars, long before the fort. It gave the island its name: Srirangapatna, the town of Sri Ranga. The deity is Vishnu reclining on the serpent Adisesha. It is the first of three great Ranganatha temples along the Kaveri, and pilgrims work down the river visiting all three. Tipu, a Muslim ruler, kept this temple running and endowed it. That inconvenient fact sits in the middle of most arguments about him. The building has Hoysala and Vijayanagara work in it.

chunks.title: Look for the reclining god in the dark
chunks.body: The inner sanctum is small and unlit except by lamps. You will not see the deity properly at first. Wait. When the priest brings the lamp round, the flame moves along the body of the reclining figure and you get it in pieces: the head, the raised hand, the serpent hoods above. That is deliberate. These sanctums were never meant to be floodlit. Stand back from the rail rather than pressing forward, and you will actually see more. The corridor around the sanctum has old pillars worth looking at on the way out.

chunks.title: The stone rings are still in the wall
chunks.body: This is a low vaulted chamber below ground level, and British prisoners were held here after Pollilur. Look at the walls. There are stone slabs with holes cut through them at about knee height. Prisoners were chained to those. The chamber floods when the river rises, which was part of the point. It is named for Colonel Baillie, who was captured in 1780 and died in captivity here in 1782. It takes ten minutes to see. It is grim and it is small and it is worth the ten minutes because it is the least varnished thing on this island.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India site marker

chunks.title: A minute is all she needs
chunks.body: Nimisha means a minute. The name of this goddess says she solves what you bring her in one minute. That is a bold promise and it is why the queue moves the way it does, with people whispering requests and going. The temple sits on the bank of the Kaveri a short way from the fort, built in the sixteenth century under the Wadiyars. It is small, it is busy, and it feels nothing like the grand sites on the island. Come here after the fort. The river is right behind and there are steps down to the water.

chunks.title: A weir people treat as a waterfall
chunks.body: Be clear about what this is before you drive out. Balmuri is a low check dam across the Kaveri, not a natural fall. Water goes over a straight concrete lip about two metres high and people stand in it. That is the whole attraction, and on a Sunday there will be several hundred people doing exactly that. It is genuinely pleasant on a hot afternoon and genuinely crowded. There is no lifeguard. The rock under the water is slippery and the current below the lip is stronger than it looks. Do not go in above the knee.

chunks.title: The last great Hoysala temple, and it is complete
chunks.body: This was finished in 1268 by Somanatha, a general under the Hoysala king Narasimha the Third. It is the last of the great Hoysala temples and, unlike Belur and Halebidu, it was finished. Three shrines on a star-shaped platform, one tower over each. Walk the outer wall clockwise. There are six horizontal bands running all the way round: elephants at the bottom for strength, then horses for speed, then foliage, then scenes from the epics, then makaras, then swans. The elephants are all different. Nobody repeated one. Count a few and check.
chunks.source_name: UNESCO Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas listing

chunks.title: Walk the platform, do not cut across
chunks.body: The temple sits on a raised star-shaped platform called a jagati, and the platform follows the shape of the building exactly. It is there so that you walk around the temple at a fixed distance, seeing every wall panel at the same angle. Do that. Do not climb up and cross the middle. It takes about fifteen minutes to go round once and it is the whole design working on you. Go in the morning, because the deep-cut carving needs low sideways light to read. At noon everything flattens out and you lose the depth.

chunks.title: No worship here, and no shoes either
chunks.body: There is no deity in the sanctums now, so this is an Archaeological Survey monument rather than a working temple. You still take your shoes off at the platform steps. It is open through the day, usually half past nine to half past five, and it is thirty-five kilometres from Mysuru along the Bannur road. Allow an hour on site and an hour of driving each way. There is no food at the site worth eating. It pairs badly with a packed day and well with a slow one. Carry water, because the platform has no shade at all.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India site information

chunks.title: The Maharani had her own railway carriage
chunks.body: There is a wooden saloon carriage here from 1899 that belonged to the Maharani of Mysore. It has a kitchen and a toilet and a royal bed. Walk through it. Then look at the ordinary third-class coach nearby and compare. This museum was set up in 1979 and it holds steam locomotives, a working turntable and a small train that runs children around the yard. It is outdoors, so morning or late afternoon. Closed Mondays. It is the best place in the city to take restless children when the palace has worn them out.
chunks.source_name: Indian Railways museum records, general reference

chunks.title: Built for one guest who came once
chunks.body: This white building went up in 1921 for a single purpose: to house the Viceroy of India when he visited. The design copies St Paul's Cathedral in London for the central dome. It is now a hotel. You can walk into the lobby, look up at the dome and the double staircase, and have a coffee without staying the night. Nobody will stop you if you are polite. It sits on rising ground east of the city with the Chamundi hill behind it, so the approach drive is the best part. Go at sunset and look back at the front.
chunks.source_name: Mysuru heritage building records, general reference

chunks.title: Walk the bund, watch the pelicans land
chunks.body: There is a walking path around this lake and a butterfly park at one end. The reason to come is the heronry: painted storks and pelicans nest on the trees on the far bank and you can watch them coming in low over the water at the end of the day. There is also a walk-through aviary, which is large but still an aviary. Closed on Tuesdays. The full loop takes about forty minutes at a slow pace and it is flat, so it works for people who cannot manage the hill or the market crowds.

chunks.title: The lake the writers walked around
chunks.body: This is where Mysuru walks. It is a tank built in 1864, inside the university campus, and it has a track around it about four and a half kilometres long. R. K. Narayan walked here. So did the poet Kuvempu. There are stone benches under old trees and a lot of birds in the winter months. Go at six in the morning or after five in the evening and you will be among students, retired professors and joggers. It is free. It is the one place in this city that belongs to the people who live here rather than to visitors.
chunks.source_name: University of Mysore campus records, general reference

chunks.title: Six and a half thousand objects nobody arranged for you
chunks.body: This is a mansion from 1905, built for a princess, now holding a folklore collection of around six and a half thousand objects: leather shadow puppets, wooden Yakshagana masks, farm tools, drums, dolls, a wooden chariot. The labelling is sparse and the lighting is bad. Come anyway. The shadow puppets are the thing to find. They are goat hide, painted, translucent, and they were worked against a lit cloth screen all night in village performances. Closed on Sundays. Give it an hour. The building alone is worth the walk if the collection is not your thing.
chunks.source_name: University of Mysore Folklore Museum records

chunks.title: Gold thread, and a stamp that means something
chunks.body: Mysore silk carries a Geographical Indication tag. The state factory here was set up in 1912 by the Maharaja with looms imported from Switzerland. What makes the sari expensive is not only the silk. It is the zari, the gold thread in the border, which uses real gold and silver. Every genuine piece carries a hologram and a code you can check. If you are buying, buy at the state showroom rather than from a shop that says it sells Mysore silk. The difference in price is real and so is the difference in the cloth.
chunks.source_name: Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation, general reference

chunks.title: One of the oldest zoos in the world
chunks.body: This zoo opened in 1892 as the Maharaja's private collection and became public later. That makes it one of the oldest in the world still running. It is large, about a hundred and fifty acres, and the enclosures are open and planted rather than barred. Allow two and a half hours minimum and expect two to three kilometres of walking. Closed on Tuesdays. Battery vehicles are available for hire if the walking is too much. Go at opening time. The animals are active early and the paths are empty for the first hour.

chunks.title: One artist, one hundred and fifteen lorry loads of sand
chunks.body: A sculptor named M. N. Gowri built everything here. The figures are made of sand and water only, no glue and no cement, and they are held up by their own compacted weight. The material came in by the lorry load. Because it is sand, it is under a roof and it cannot be touched. That is why the ropes are there. It sits on the Chamundi Hill road, so it fits naturally on the way up or down. Twenty minutes is enough. It is a small, cheerful, slightly odd stop that works well with children.

chunks.title: Why this city smells different
chunks.body: Stop somewhere in the old part of the city and breathe in properly. There are three smells layered here and each has a reason. Jasmine, because Mysore mallige grows in the fields just outside and comes into Devaraja Market before dawn. Sandalwood, because the Mysore kings held a monopoly on it and built an oil factory here in 1916. And incense, because those two industries made this a natural place to roll agarbatti, which the city still does at scale. The smell of Mysuru is an industrial history you can breathe.

chunks.title: Buy your dosa where the queue is local
chunks.body: Mysuru has a specific breakfast grammar. The dosa is soft and thick, not crisp. It is served with white coconut chutney and no sambar. There is more ghee than you expect and that is not an accident, it is the dish. The good places are small, cash-heavy, open early and closed by late morning. If a place is open at three in the afternoon serving dosa, it is serving something else. Mylari in Nazarbad is the name people argue about. There are two shops with similar names on the same stretch and locals have strong opinions about which is the real one.

chunks.title: Three earlier palaces stood where you are standing
chunks.body: Count them. The first palace on this ground was a wooden fort building from the fourteenth century. It was struck by lightning in 1638 and rebuilt. That second one was pulled down and rebuilt again in 1793 after the Wadiyars returned to power. The third burned in 1897. The one you can see is the fourth. Each was built on the ruins of the last because the site was fixed by the temples inside the walls, not by convenience. That is why the palace is where it is, in the middle of the traffic, rather than on a comfortable hill.
chunks.source_name: Maps of India, The Royal History of Mysore Palace

chunks.title: Dasara is ten days, not one
chunks.body: If you are here in September or October, know how the festival is shaped. It runs ten days. The first nine are worship, music and wrestling, spread across the palace, the hill and venues around the city. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, is the procession: caparisoned elephants, the golden howdah, a route from the palace to the Bannimantap grounds, and a torchlight parade in the evening. Hotel rates triple and the roads shut. If you want the spectacle, book months ahead. If you want the city, come in November instead. The wrestling bouts through the week are free to watch.

chunks.title: The chariot is on the back of the fifty rupee note
chunks.body: Take out a fifty rupee note and look at the back. That stone chariot is the one in front of you. It is a shrine to Garuda, the eagle who carries Vishnu, and it is built as a temple car made of stone. The wheels used to turn. They were cemented in place some years ago because people kept spinning them and the stone was wearing. It is not carved from a single rock, whatever you are told. It is blocks, fitted so well that the joints are hard to find. Walk round the back and look for them.

chunks.title: Fifty-six pillars that were tuned
chunks.body: In the great hall to the east there is a cluster of slender pillars around the thicker ones. They are cut from single blocks of resonant stone and each one sounds a different note when struck. People call them the saregama pillars. You cannot tap them now. Decades of tapping cracked several, so the Archaeological Survey has stopped it. Look instead. Notice the pillars are different thicknesses and lengths. That is the tuning. Someone tested the rock, cut it, tested it again. This is stone masonry doing the job of instrument making.

chunks.title: Krishnadevaraya saw a chariot and wanted one
chunks.body: The story told here is that Krishnadevaraya came back from a campaign in Odisha having seen the temple at Konark with its stone wheels, and decided he would have one too. The Vittala complex was already being built. He expanded it and added the chariot. Whether the Konark link is true or a good story attached later, the pattern is real: this king took what he saw on campaign and put it in his capital. The temple was never fully consecrated. Work stopped, and then in 1565 there was no more work to be done.

chunks.title: Stand at the east end of the hall and look along it
chunks.body: Go to the far east end of the main pillared hall, stand in the centre, and look back along the axis. The pillars line up in avenues and the ceiling opens above you in carved panels. Each of the big composite pillars is a bundle: a central shaft with attached colonnettes, and animals carved at the base. Find the ones with yalis, the lion-like creatures with riders. Then look at the ceiling directly overhead. The lotus medallions are cut so deep that the shadow does the work. Morning light, coming in low from the east, is when this hall is best.

chunks.title: The bazaar in front was a market street
chunks.body: Walk out of the east gate and look at the long avenue running away from you with colonnades on both sides. That is not a ruin of houses. It was a market street, over half a kilometre long, and traders sold there under those stone roofs. Portuguese visitors described gems being sold openly by the heap in streets like this. Walk a hundred metres down it and turn round. From there you get the temple gopura framed by the colonnade, which is how it was meant to be approached. Almost nobody walks this far. It is the quietest good view at Hampi.
chunks.source_name: BA Notes, Paes and Nuniz on Vijayanagara

chunks.title: The buggy, the walk, and the heat
chunks.body: You cannot drive to the Vittala temple. Vehicles stop about a kilometre and a half away and you either walk or take the battery buggy that shuttles from the car park. Take the buggy on the way in if it is hot, walk back if you can, because the walk passes the old bazaar. The site usually opens around half past eight and closes at half past five. There is almost no shade inside the complex. Go before ten or after four. Midday here in April is genuinely dangerous, not just uncomfortable.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site information

chunks.title: One ticket covers this and the Lotus Mahal
chunks.body: The Vittala complex is a ticketed Archaeological Survey site, and the same ticket usually covers the Zenana enclosure with the Lotus Mahal and the Elephant Stables on the same day. Keep the stub. Buy online if you can, the queue at the gate is slow in season. Indian and foreign nationals pay different rates, and children under fifteen are usually free. Bring the receipt on your phone as well as printed, because the network drops in and out around the river. Children under fifteen usually enter free, but carry something that proves the age.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi ticketing

chunks.title: Where the deity went when the army came
chunks.body: The Vittala image is not here. Before the sack of 1565 the deity was moved out, and Vitthala is worshipped at Pandharpur in Maharashtra, where the tradition holds that the image came from Hampi and went back. So this vast complex is empty by design now, not only by damage. That is why it feels like architecture rather than a temple when you stand in it. There is no bell, no queue, no oil lamp. What survives is the building thinking out loud about stone. The silence here is administrative rather than spiritual.

chunks.title: Look for the burn marks
chunks.body: On some of the pillars and lintels here the granite has a pinkish, flaked, crumbly look, quite different from the smooth grey elsewhere. That is fire damage. Granite spalls when it is heated hard and then cooled. After Talikota the city was worked over for months and fire was one of the tools. You are looking at the physical record of that. Once you learn to see it you will find it across Hampi, on the Krishna temple, on the Achyutaraya complex. It is the difference between a building that fell down and a building that was destroyed.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi conservation notes

chunks.title: Bring water in, there is nothing to buy
chunks.body: There are no stalls inside the Vittala complex and the ones at the drop-off point are limited. Carry at least a litre a person. There is no proper food nearby either. The nearest reliable meal is back in Hampi Bazaar or across at the Mango Tree. If you are doing Vittala in the morning, eat first at your guesthouse and plan lunch for after. Doing this site hungry, in the sun, with a small child, is how good days go wrong here. A hat and a packet of salt biscuits are worth carrying too, and so is a spare bottle for the walk back.

chunks.title: Worship here has not stopped in twelve hundred years
chunks.body: Everything else at Hampi is a ruin. This is not. Virupaksha has been a working temple since about the seventh century and it never closed, not after Talikota, not after the city emptied. The army that broke this capital in 1565 left this temple standing and in use. Walk in past the tall gopura and there is a priest, a queue, a bell, an elephant. Whatever you think of the rest of the site, understand that you are stepping into a building that has been doing the same job continuously for twelve hundred years.

chunks.title: Pampa, Pampapathi, Hampi
chunks.body: The local goddess here is Pampa, a river goddess, and Shiva married her. As her husband he is Pampapathi, lord of Pampa. The place took her name: Pampa-kshetra, worn down over centuries into Hampi. So the name of this town is the name of a goddess, shortened. Virupaksha is Shiva's other name here, the one with oblique eyes. The annual marriage festival of Virupaksha and Pampa is still celebrated and it fills these courtyards. The name of the ruin field you have come to photograph is really the name of a wedding.

chunks.title: The upside-down tower on the wall
chunks.body: Go into the inner courtyard, find the small dark chamber on the west side, and wait for your eyes to adjust. On the back wall there is an image of the main gopura, upside down. It is not painted. It comes through a small hole in the opposite wall. The whole temple gateway is being projected onto that wall by a pinhole. Somebody built a working camera obscura into a temple, either on purpose or by accident, hundreds of years ago. It is faint. Give it two minutes in the dark and it appears.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The gopura is nine storeys and it leans on old bones
chunks.body: The eastern tower is about fifty metres high, nine tiers of brick and plaster figures on a stone base. Lakkana Dandesha, a chieftain under Deva Raya the Second, built the central hall and this gateway in the fifteenth century. The shrine at the core is far older. That is the pattern again: an old, small, dark sanctum with successive kings piling height on the outside. Stand at the far end of the bazaar street and look back. The tower is designed to be read from a distance, which is why the detail gets bigger as it goes up.

chunks.title: Lakshmi the elephant, and the rules about her
chunks.body: There is usually a temple elephant here who will take a coin and touch your head. Understand what you are joining in. She is a working animal in a hot stone courtyard. If you want to see her at her best, go early, around seven, when she is taken down to the river to be bathed. That happens on the steps below the temple and it is free, unhurried and much better than the courtyard transaction. Some visitors choose not to pay for the blessing at all. That is a reasonable choice and nobody will mind.

chunks.title: Barefoot from the gate, and mind the monkeys
chunks.body: Shoes come off at the outer gate, not at the sanctum, so you will be walking a long way on stone. Between eleven and four that stone is very hot. There is a shoe counter and a small fee. Cameras are allowed in the courtyards but not in the inner sanctum. The monkeys here are bold and they take food, water bottles, sunglasses and phones. Do not hold anything loosely in an outstretched hand. The temple is usually open early morning to midday and again from late afternoon. A pair of socks helps on the hot stone.

chunks.title: The painted ceiling nobody looks up at
chunks.body: In the main hall, stop and look straight up. The ceiling is painted, and the paint is old. There are scenes from the epics and a panel showing the sage Vidyaranya being carried in a procession. The colours have gone brown and the surface is sooty from centuries of lamps, so it does not announce itself. Stand under it, let your eyes settle, and the figures come out of the dark. Most people walk this hall looking at the floor because of the crowd. Look up. It is the oldest painted surface you will see at Hampi.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Free to enter, and that matters here
chunks.body: There is no ticket to enter Virupaksha. There is a small charge for the camera and for the shoe counter. That is worth saying because Hampi is otherwise a ticketed archaeological landscape, and this one building is still a place of worship funded as a temple. If you are on a tight budget or a short stop, this is the site to prioritise. It is also the one that will be busiest with pilgrims rather than tourists, particularly on Mondays, which are Shiva's day. Dress as you would for any working temple, shoulders and knees covered.

chunks.title: Climb Hemakuta at dusk and look down on the roof
chunks.body: Directly behind and above the temple is Hemakuta hill, a low slope covered in small stone shrines. It is a five-minute climb from beside the temple gate. From up there you look down on the gopura and out across the boulder field to the river. The stone goes orange in the last half hour of light. This is the standard evening thing to do in Hampi and it is standard because it is right. Take a torch for coming down. The path has loose steps and the light goes fast here.

chunks.title: Eat on the bazaar street after the morning visit
chunks.body: The street running east from the temple was the old chariot street and it now has small cafes at the near end. This is where you get the standard Hampi traveller breakfast: fruit, curd, toast, a decent coffee. For local food rather than traveller food, ask for the small places behind the bazaar serving rice, sambar and a chilli-heavy palya at midday. Hampi is a temple town, so alcohol is restricted and much of the eating is vegetarian. Plan around that rather than being surprised by it. Carry small notes, because card machines here are unreliable.

chunks.title: Two brothers, one river, 1336
chunks.body: In 1336 two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded a city on the south bank of the Tungabhadra. That is the start of the Vijayanagara empire. They were officers who had been taken north as prisoners and came back to build a state that would hold the Deccan against the Delhi Sultanate. It worked for two hundred and thirty years. At its height the empire ran from the Krishna river to the southern tip of the peninsula. The boulders you are standing among were the capital of the largest kingdom in the south.

chunks.title: One battle, and then five months of taking the city apart
chunks.body: On the twenty-sixth of January 1565 the Vijayanagara army met a coalition of Deccan sultanates at Talikota. Vijayanagara lost. The regent Rama Raya was captured and killed on the field. Then the victors came to the capital. What followed was not a night of looting. Accounts describe months of systematic demolition: temples broken, images smashed, buildings fired. The city was never reoccupied. That is why Hampi is what it is. Most ruined cities decay. This one was taken apart by hand, and then simply left. No later dynasty tried to rebuild on the site.

chunks.title: A Portuguese horse trader wrote it all down
chunks.body: Around 1520 a Portuguese man named Domingo Paes walked these streets and wrote what he saw. He said the city was as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world. He described markets stocked with every grain and spice, and rubies and diamonds and pearls sold openly in the bazaars by the heap. A decade or so later Fernao Nuniz wrote a second account. Between them, those two traders are our closest eyewitness record. When you stand in an empty colonnade here, that is what you are standing in.
chunks.source_name: BA Notes, Paes and Nuniz on Vijayanagara

chunks.title: Krishnadevaraya, 1509 to 1529
chunks.body: If Hampi has a high-water mark it is these twenty years. Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva line took the throne in 1509. He won campaigns north into Gulbarga and Bidar and east into Odisha, he rebuilt and endowed temples across the empire, and he wrote poetry in Telugu himself. Most of the building you will photograph here was raised or extended under him: the Vittala expansions, the Krishna temple, the Hazara Rama refinements. He died in 1529. Thirty-six years later the empire was gone. That is how narrow the window was.

chunks.title: Hanuman was born on that hill
chunks.body: Look north across the river at the hill with the white temple on top. Tradition holds that Hanuman was born there, to his mother Anjana, which is why it is called Anjanadri. This whole landscape is identified with Kishkindha, the monkey kingdom of the Ramayana, where Rama met Sugriva and Hanuman. The boulders are said to be what is left of a fight between two brothers. You can climb it. There are about five hundred and seventy steps to the top and the view back over the river and the boulder field is the best in the region.

chunks.title: Five hundred and seventy steps, and no shade
chunks.body: The climb takes thirty to forty-five minutes at a steady pace. There is a handrail most of the way and the steps are uneven. There is very little shade. Do this at sunrise or in the last two hours of daylight and not otherwise. Monkeys are everywhere on the upper section and they will take anything you carry loosely. If anyone in the group has knee trouble or a heart condition, this is the one to skip: the descent is harder than the climb and there is no vehicle access above the base.

chunks.title: The older town on the other bank
chunks.body: Anegundi is across the river and it is older than Hampi. Before Harihara and Bukka built the new capital on the south bank, this was the settlement. It is still a working village rather than a monument: houses, fields, a fort wall, temples in daily use, banana plantations. Local tradition puts Kishkindha here. Go for half a day and walk. The contrast with the south bank is the point. On one side an empty archaeological landscape, on the other the same landscape with people living in it. A motorised ferry crosses when the river is low enough to allow it.

chunks.title: A round basket boat that has not changed
chunks.body: The coracle is a bowl of woven bamboo, waterproofed, about two metres across, with no bow and no stern. It spins as it goes and it cannot be steered in a straight line. That is not bad boatmanship, it is the design. The shape works because this river is shallow and full of rock, and a round hull bounces off instead of catching. Boats like this are described in accounts of the Vijayanagara river crossings. Sit down in the middle, keep your weight low, and let the boatman work. Do not stand up while it is moving.

chunks.title: Late afternoon on the water, near the Vittala end
chunks.body: The best stretch is the one below the Vittala temple, where the old stone bridge piers stand in the water and there are carved lingas cut into the rock at the river's edge. Go in the last hour of light. The rock is warm, the water is dark, and the boatman will spin the coracle on purpose to make you laugh, which is part of the deal. Agree the price and the length of the ride before you get in. Life jackets are not always offered. Ask for one. Bring a dry bag for your phone.

chunks.title: The highest point, and the best sunrise
chunks.body: Matanga is the highest hill inside the Hampi site, and from the small temple on top you can see the whole city plan at once: Virupaksha and its bazaar to the west, the Achyutaraya complex and its street below you, the river curving north, the Vittala road east. Named for the sage Matanga, whose hermitage the Ramayana places here. The climb from the Achyutaraya side takes about twenty-five minutes. Start in the dark for sunrise. Do not do the descent in the dark, and do not do this route alone at dawn; go with company or a guide.

chunks.title: A building that is neither temple nor mosque
chunks.body: Look at the arches. They are lobed, cusped, Islamic in shape. Now look at the roof. It is a set of pyramidal towers, straight out of a Hindu temple. This building does both at once and it was not confused about it. The Vijayanagara court employed Muslim officers and architects and borrowed freely. The name Lotus Mahal is modern, from the shape of the arches and the plan. What it was actually for is not certain: a council chamber, or a room in the women's quarter where the court could sit in the cool. Two storeys, open on all sides, built to move air.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Why this one survived the sack
chunks.body: Almost every religious building here was broken. This one was not. Look around the enclosure at the watchtowers and the high wall. It is a secular building inside a guarded compound, and it had no images in it to smash. The army that came in 1565 had a target list, and it was images and temples. Buildings with no god inside them were mostly left. That is why the Elephant Stables next door are intact too, and why the Vittala hall is broken. What survives at Hampi is not random. It is a map of what the destroyers cared about.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi conservation notes

chunks.title: Eleven domes, and no two the same
chunks.body: Count the chambers. Eleven, in a long row, each with a big arched door and a dome on top. Now look along the roofline. The domes alternate: ribbed, fluted, plain, octagonal. Nobody had to do that. A stable does not need variety. The central chamber is larger, with a raised platform above it, probably for musicians during processions. Each bay held one elephant, and there are hooks in the ceilings where the chains ran. Stand at one end and sight down the row. The rhythm of the domes is the whole point of the building.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The goddess who was broken off his lap
chunks.body: This is the largest single sculpture at Hampi, over six metres, cut in 1528 under Krishnadevaraya. Narasimha, the man-lion, sits cross-legged under a seven-hooded serpent. Look at his left thigh. There is a hand resting on it that does not belong to him. That is all that remains of Lakshmi, who sat on his knee. She was broken off in 1565. You can still see where she was. The figure was also once framed by an arch that is now gone. What you are looking at is a fragment being presented as a monument.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Standing in water, and always has been
chunks.body: Next door to Narasimha is a chamber holding a linga three metres high, with its base permanently in water. A channel feeds it. The name means the poor man's linga: the story is that it was commissioned by a peasant woman, which is unusual, since almost everything here was royal. Look at the top of the linga. There are three horizontal marks cut into it representing the eyes of Shiva. The chamber is open to the sky. Stand at the door and look in rather than crowding the small space.

chunks.title: The platform the king watched the empire from
chunks.body: This is a stepped stone platform about eight metres high, and from the top of it the king watched the Mahanavami festival: processions, wrestling, dancing, military review. Domingo Paes described those nine days in detail. Walk round the base before you climb it. The sides are carved in horizontal bands with hunting scenes, dancers, horses, camels, and foreign traders in hats and long coats. Those figures with the odd headgear are Portuguese and Arab. The empire is describing its own trade partners on the wall of its ceremonial platform. Climb it last, after you have read the four sides.
chunks.source_name: BA Notes, Paes and Nuniz on Vijayanagara

chunks.title: A tank found buried in the 1980s
chunks.body: This tank was under earth until excavation in the 1980s uncovered it. It is a square pit lined with five tiers of steps going down, built in black schist rather than the local granite. That stone is not from here. It was quarried elsewhere and brought in, and the blocks carry mason's marks and numbers, which means it was cut to plan somewhere else and assembled here like a kit. Walk round all four sides. The geometry only resolves from the corners. Water reached it through a stone aqueduct you can still trace across the enclosure.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi excavation records

chunks.title: Plain outside, and that is the trick
chunks.body: From the road this looks like a blank rectangular box. Go in. There is a large sunken bath in the middle, open to the sky, ringed by a vaulted corridor with projecting balconies looking down into the water. The ceilings of that corridor are worked in plaster. There was a moat around the whole building. Nobody is sure the queen ever bathed here; the name is later. Stand on one of the balconies and look across. Every balcony has a different stucco ceiling. It takes ten minutes and it is right next to the road.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The whole Ramayana, on a wall, in order
chunks.body: This was the private chapel of the royal family, right inside the royal enclosure. The outer wall carries the Ramayana in horizontal registers, and you read it by walking. Start at the north side and go clockwise. Rama's birth, the bow, the exile, the golden deer, the abduction, the alliance with the monkeys, the bridge, the battle, the return. The name means a thousand Ramas. Inside, four polished black pillars carry scenes from the Krishna story. This is the best-preserved narrative surface at Hampi and it takes twenty unhurried minutes.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Why the king kept the Ramayana next to his bedroom
chunks.body: Putting the Ramayana on the wall of the palace chapel is a political statement, not only a devotional one. Rama is the model king: exiled, patient, victorious, just. A dynasty that had come out of nowhere in 1336 to hold the south against the sultanates had a use for that comparison. And the landscape helped. Hampi was already identified with Kishkindha, where Rama found his allies. So the king was living inside the geography of the poem and carving the poem on his own walls. That is careful work. Read the wall as propaganda and it gets sharper.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The mustard seed Ganesha and the snake belt
chunks.body: Sasivekalu means mustard seed. This Ganesha is over two metres high and carved from one boulder, and the name comes from a story: Ganesha ate so much that his stomach threatened to burst, so he tied a snake around it. Walk round to the back. The snake is there, carved across the belly. The open pavilion around him is a later addition. He was commissioned in 1506 in memory of a king, Narasimha the Second, according to an inscription nearby. Five minutes on the way up Hemakuta hill. The pavilion columns around him are later work, and plainer.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Named for a stomach that looks like a chickpea
chunks.body: Kadalekalu means gram, the chickpea, and the name comes from the shape of the belly. This one is around four and a half metres high, taller than the mustard seed Ganesha, carved out of a boulder in place on the hillside. The pillared hall in front of it is large, with tall slender columns, and it was built around the finished sculpture. Look at the hall floor: it is bare rock, levelled where needed and left where it was already flat. Vijayanagara builders worked with the boulders rather than clearing them.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The oldest buildings on the site are the plainest
chunks.body: These small shrines are older than the Vijayanagara empire, mostly ninth to fourteenth century, and several are pre-Vijayanagara Jain and Shaiva temples. They look nothing like Vittala. No figure carving, no gopura, just square cells with stepped pyramidal roofs in plain granite. That austerity is the earlier style. Walk among them and then go and look at Vittala, and you can see three hundred years of increasing confidence and increasing money. The hill is a short easy climb from beside Virupaksha and it is the best place in Hampi at sunset.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Built for a victory, and the idol went to Chennai
chunks.body: Krishnadevaraya built this in 1513 after taking Udayagiri in Odisha. He brought back an image of Balakrishna as war booty and installed it here. That image is not here now. It is in the Government Museum in Chennai. The temple has a broken gopura, a large courtyard and a long ruined bazaar street running east with a stone tank at the far end. Look at the eastern gopura base: the plaster figures on it include scenes from the campaign. A temple built to commemorate a conquest, holding a god who was part of the loot.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The last big temple built here
chunks.body: This went up in 1534, under Achyuta Deva Raya, and it is the last major temple complex built at Vijayanagara. Thirty-one years later the city was finished. It sits in a valley between Matanga hill and Gandhamadana hill, with a long colonnaded bazaar street running north from it towards the river. Because it is a walk from the road it is one of the emptiest large sites here. Go in the morning. Walk the bazaar street first, from the far end, so you approach the temple the way the traders did.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: The king was weighed against gold
chunks.body: This is a stone arch with hooks in the crossbeam. On certain days the king sat in a pan on one side and gold, silver or grain was piled on the other until it balanced, and then that weight was given away to the temple and the priests. It is called tula purushadana. Look at the loops carved into the underside of the beam. Simple, heavy, and completely legible as a machine. It stands on the road between the Vittala temple and the river. Two minutes, and it tells you more about how kingship worked here than a palace does.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: Where Rama waited out the rains
chunks.body: The Ramayana places Rama and Lakshmana on this hill through the monsoon, waiting for the season to end before the search for Sita could go on. The temple here is built around the boulders rather than on cleared ground, and the rock comes up through the floor inside the sanctum. Go round the back of the hill and you will find rows of lingas cut into the bare rock surface, hundreds of them. It is quiet, it is off the main circuit, and it is the best place here to understand that Hampi was a sacred landscape long before it was a capital.
chunks.source_name: Ramayana tradition and local practice, general reference

chunks.title: A large ruin with nobody in it
chunks.body: This is one of the biggest temple complexes at Hampi and one of the least visited, because it is out near Kamalapura rather than in the main circuit. Large courtyard, tall gopura, a long pillared hall, and quite often not another person in it. If you have had enough of crowds at Virupaksha, come here in the late afternoon. The hall is deep enough to be cool. There is no ticket and no guide and very little signage, which is either the drawback or the appeal depending on your mood.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi site notes

chunks.title: See the model first, then the ruins make sense
chunks.body: There is a scale model of the entire Vijayanagara site in this museum. Go and stand over it before you spend two days walking around confused. It shows how the sacred centre by the river, the royal centre near Kamalapura and the suburbs relate to each other, which is almost impossible to work out on the ground. The galleries hold sculpture, hero stones, coins and excavated metalwork. It is small, air-conditioned and cheap. Closed on Fridays. Do it on your first morning, not your last. Photography inside the galleries is usually not allowed.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hampi museum information

chunks.title: Green water in a granite bowl
chunks.body: This is a reservoir on the north side of the river, past Anegundi, fed by a canal from the Tungabhadra dam. The water sits between bare grey boulders and it goes an intense green in the right light. People swim here and people ride coracles on it. There are no lifeguards and the sides shelve steeply. If you swim, stay near the edge and go with someone. It is about a forty-minute ride from Hampi bazaar via the bridge at Bukkasagara or the ferry, and the ride out through the banana fields is half the pleasure.

chunks.title: The dam that changed the river below Hampi
chunks.body: This dam was completed in 1953, about fifteen kilometres upstream of Hampi near Hospet. It irrigates a large part of this district and it is the reason the banana and sugarcane fields you drove past exist. It also regulates what the river does at Hampi. Before it, the Tungabhadra swung between a torrent and a trickle. There is a garden below the dam with musical fountains in the evening. Go for the view along the reservoir at sunset rather than for the fountains, which are ordinary. Security on the dam wall is strict, so leave drones behind.

chunks.title: Bears on a rock at five in the evening
chunks.body: This sanctuary was set up in 1994 on scrub and boulder country about fifteen kilometres from Hampi, and it protects Indian sloth bears. There is a viewing platform, and honey is put out on a rock face in the late afternoon to draw the bears into view. They usually come out around half past four to six. Take binoculars. Go in the evening slot, not the morning. Sightings are common but not guaranteed, and the drive is about forty-five minutes each way, so treat it as an evening rather than a quick stop.
chunks.source_name: Karnataka Forest Department, Daroji sanctuary records

chunks.title: Thali on the floor, river outside
chunks.body: This is the traveller institution in Hampi. You sit low, often on mats, and the standard order is the thali: rice, sambar, rasam, two vegetable dishes, curd, papad, a sweet. It is unhurried, which is either restful or maddening depending on your schedule. Order and then go and look at the view rather than watching the kitchen door. It is vegetarian, like most of Hampi. If you want the local rather than the traveller version of the same meal, the small places behind the bazaar do it for a third of the price.

chunks.title: A market street that was cleared out
chunks.body: The colonnades running east from Virupaksha were the old chariot street, and until 2011 people lived and traded in them. Families had been there for generations. They were moved out as part of the World Heritage conservation plan and resettled nearby. Walk the street now and you will see the stone shells with nothing in them. Whether that was the right call is genuinely argued, here and elsewhere. What you are looking at is a heritage decision, made recently, not a ruin from 1565. Ask a shopkeeper here about it and you will get a straight answer, one way or the other.
chunks.source_name: UNESCO Hampi conservation records, general reference

chunks.title: Eat the banana, it grew across the road
chunks.body: The fields between Hampi and the river are banana and sugarcane, fed by the Tungabhadra canals. Buy bananas from a roadside seller rather than a cafe. There are several varieties here and the small, thick-skinned yellow ones are sweeter than the long export type. On the same stalls you will find fresh sugarcane juice pressed with lime and ginger, which is the right thing to drink at four in the afternoon between temples. Ask for it without ice if you are careful about water. A tender coconut from the same stall rehydrates you better than any soft drink will.

chunks.title: How to divide the site into days
chunks.body: Hampi is not one place, it is about twenty-six square kilometres. Split it. Morning one: Virupaksha, Hemakuta, the Kadalekalu and Sasivekalu Ganeshas, the bazaar street. Afternoon one: the royal centre, so Mahanavami Dibba, the stepped tank, Hazara Rama, Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, and the museum at Kamalapura. Morning two: Vittala, the King's Balance, the river path, a coracle. Afternoon two: cross to Anegundi and Anjanadri. Hire a bicycle or a scooter or an auto for the day. Walking the whole thing is not realistic in the heat. Two full days is the minimum that works.

chunks.title: When to come, and when not to
chunks.body: November to February is the window. Days are warm and the evenings are cool. March starts to bite and by April and May the granite radiates heat well into the night, with days over forty degrees. The monsoon, June to September, is green and the river is full but many of the rock climbs get slippery. Whatever month you come, the working day here is early morning and late afternoon, with the middle four hours spent indoors. Plan around that and Hampi is easy. Ignore it and it is punishing.

chunks.title: Why the boulders are here at all
chunks.body: Look at the landscape properly for a moment. Those rounded granite boulders piled on each other are among the oldest exposed rock on the planet, in the region of two and a half to three billion years old. They were never stacked. They are a single mass of granite that weathered along its natural joints, so the corners rounded off and the blocks separated in place. The Vijayanagara builders quarried them by drilling a line of holes and splitting with wedges. You can find half-split boulders with the drill holes still in them all over the site.
chunks.source_name: Geological Survey of India, Dharwar craton, general reference

chunks.title: The stone that will not let go of the heat
chunks.body: Put your palm on a boulder at eight in the evening in April. It is still warm. Granite takes heat all day and gives it back all night, which is why Hampi feels hotter after dark than the air temperature says.
