That single fact shapes everything: why the old buildings are open pavilions rather than closed rooms, why the halls are deep and shaded, why the tanks and channels run everywhere. The city was engineered against this rock. When you stand in the Lotus Mahal and feel the draught, that is the answer to the boulder you just touched.

chunks.title: An empty capital, and why nobody came back
chunks.body: Cities usually recover. This one did not. After 1565 the court moved south to Penukonda and then Chandragiri, the trade routes shifted, and the irrigation works that fed a quarter of a million people fell out of repair. Without the canals the land could not hold the population. So the ruin you are walking through is not only the work of an army. It is what happens when the water system behind a city stops being maintained. Look for the stone aqueducts and channels as you walk. They are the reason there was ever a city here.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Vijayanagara research reports

chunks.title: One temple, one hundred and three years
chunks.body: The Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana consecrated this in 1117 to mark beating the Cholas at Talakad. He called it Vijaya Narayana. But it was not finished in his lifetime, or his son's. Work carried on for about a hundred and three years and it was his grandson, Veera Ballala the Second, who saw the end of it. Three generations of one family paid stonemasons to keep going on one building. Stand at the front and take that in before you look at any detail. Everything you are about to see was cut by hand, over a century, on a single commission.

chunks.title: The men who signed the stone
chunks.body: Hoysala sculptors put their names on their work. The master craftsmen here were Dasoja and his son Chavana, from Balligavi in what is now Shivamogga district, a centre of Chalukya art. Look at the base of the bracket figures and the pillar capitals and you will find short inscriptions in old Kannada. That is a signature. This matters, because in most of medieval India we have no idea who carved anything. Here the men are named, the fathers and sons are recorded, and in some cases you can follow one hand from bracket to bracket.

chunks.title: Darpana Sundari, the lady with the mirror
chunks.body: Of the bracket figures on this temple, one is the one everybody comes for. She is called Darpana Sundari, the beauty with the mirror, and she stands holding it up and looking into it. Local tradition says the model was Shantala Devi, Vishnuvardhana's queen, herself a trained dancer. Look at what the sculptor did with her weight: hip thrown out, one heel raised, the whole body in a curve. Then look at the mirror. It is turned towards her, not towards you. You are watching someone who is not performing for you.

chunks.title: Forty-two brackets, and what to look for
chunks.body: The bracket figures, madanikas or shilabalikas, sit high up under the eaves at an angle. There are more than forty. They are dancers, hunters, a woman with a parrot, a woman pulling a thorn from her foot, a woman with a monkey tugging at her clothes. Each one is cut almost free of the wall, held on by a thin stone strut. Look for the drill work: the necklaces have separate beads with holes through them, and on some figures a chain hangs loose from the stone. Those were made by drilling into solid rock and cutting away from inside.

chunks.title: Walk in and look for the lathe-turned pillars
chunks.body: Inside the main hall there are forty-eight pillars and no two are the same. Several of them were turned, not carved. The stone was rotated against a fixed cutting edge, the way you turn wood on a lathe, which is why the mouldings are perfectly circular and the surface is polished. The Narasimha pillar at the centre is the famous one, covered in miniature figures, and it is said to have once rotated on its own base. Put your eye level with a pillar and sight along it. The rings are true.

chunks.title: Twenty-four Vishnus that change through the day
chunks.body: The sanctum is star-shaped, so its outer wall zigzags. On it are twenty-four forms of Vishnu. Because the wall folds in and out, each figure is lit from a different angle and the sun moves across them through the day, so the set never looks the same twice. That is not an accident of the plan. The star shape exists to make more wall and to make more angles. Walk the full circuit at ten in the morning, then again at four if you can, and compare. It is the same building doing two different things.

chunks.title: Still a working temple, so cover up
chunks.body: This is not a dead monument. Daily worship continues here and has done for nine hundred years. That means shoes off at the entrance to the compound, shoulders and knees covered, and the sanctum closed during the midday break, usually around one to three. The complex is generally open from about half past seven in the morning to half past seven at night. Go early. The tour buses arrive from Hassan mid-morning and the compound is small enough that fifty extra people change the experience. A guide will expect the same of you and will say so at the gate.

chunks.title: Hire the guide, this once
chunks.body: Normally you can skip the guide. Not here. The carving is dense, it is high up, much of it is small, and without someone pointing you will walk past ninety percent of it. Take a licensed guide from the counter at the gate and agree the price first. Ask specifically for the erotic panels on the lower band, the Darpana Sundari, the drilled chains, and the panel where the same figure reads as different animals from different angles. An hour with a guide here is worth three hours alone. Agree the language before you start.

chunks.title: The gopura is not Hoysala
chunks.body: The tall brick and plaster gateway you walked through does not match the temple. It is Vijayanagara work, added in the sixteenth century, four hundred years after the temple. Once you know that, the whole compound reads correctly: a low, wide, dark, densely carved stone building from the twelfth century, with a tall painted tower stuck on the front by a later empire that wanted its name here too. Turn round at the temple steps and look back at the gopura. The two buildings are not speaking the same language.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Belur site notes

chunks.title: Eat in Belur town, not at the gate
chunks.body: The stalls immediately outside the temple sell soft drinks and packet snacks. Walk two minutes into Belur town and you will find small darshini places doing idli, vada and a strong filter coffee for very little. Order the coffee by asking for a bai two, which means it comes split between the tumbler and the bowl for cooling. If you are driving on to Halebidu, eat here first. Halebidu is smaller and has less choice, and the two temples together take longer than people plan for. Carry cash, because many of these places do not take cards.

chunks.title: Strike, Sala
chunks.body: A young man called Sala was standing with his Jain teacher near a temple of the goddess Vasantika at Sosevur when a tiger came out. The teacher shouted two words: poy, Sala. Strike, Sala. He struck, and killed it, and the dynasty took its name from the command. Hoy is strike in old Kannada. Hoy-sala. You will see it as the royal emblem everywhere in these temples: a young man with a dagger over a tiger. There is a harder reading too. The tiger was the emblem of the Cholas, and Vishnuvardhana beat the Cholas at Talakad in 1116, a year before Belur was consecrated.
chunks.source_name: Belur inscription of Vishnuvardhana, c. 1117, general reference

chunks.title: Jakanachari, and the son who found the flaw
chunks.body: The story goes that Jakanachari was the greatest sculptor of his age. Working at Belur, he finished an image and a young man appeared and said there was a flaw in it: a hollow inside the stone with a frog and water. Jakanachari swore he would cut off his own hand if it were true. They opened the stone. There was a hollow. He cut off his hand. Then he learned the young man was his own son Dankanachari, whom he had left before birth. Scholars now think Jakanachari was never one man but a guild name, used across three centuries. The story survives anyway, because it is about what a craftsman owes the stone.

chunks.title: Soft when it comes out of the ground
chunks.body: None of this carving would be possible in granite. Hoysala temples are built in chloritic schist, which people call soapstone. When it is quarried it is soft enough to work with a fine tool, soft enough to drill and undercut and turn on a lathe. Exposed to air over years it hardens. So the sculptors got wood-like workability and then the material set into something that could stand outdoors for nine hundred years. That is the whole technical secret of Belur and Halebidu. It is not that these carvers were better. It is that they had a better stone.
chunks.source_name: India That Was, The Hoysaleswara Temple Halebidu

chunks.title: Why Hoysala temples are low and wide
chunks.body: Compare these with a north Indian temple and the difference is the height. Hoysala buildings spread sideways rather than up. They sit on a raised star-shaped platform, the jagati, which follows the outline of the building so you can walk round it at a constant distance. The tower over the sanctum is short and stepped. The reason is partly the stone: soapstone is not strong enough for great height. The result is a building designed to be read close up and in the round, panel by panel, rather than seen from far away.
chunks.source_name: UNESCO Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas listing, general reference

chunks.title: World Heritage, and only since 2023
chunks.body: The Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023 under the name Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. They had been on the tentative list since 2014. That is late. Hampi was listed in 1986. What it means practically is that conservation funding and visitor management here are still being built out, so signage is thin and the sites are less organised than Hampi. It also means fewer people. Come now rather than in ten years. The listing covers three temples rather than one, so ticketing is separate at each.
chunks.source_name: UNESCO World Heritage List, Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas

chunks.title: The temple that was never finished
chunks.body: Work started here around 1121 and it never stopped, and it never ended either. The tower over the sanctum was never built. Look at the roofline: it is flat where it should rise. Money and time kept going in for over a century and then in 1311 Malik Kafur came down from Delhi, and again in 1327, and the capital was sacked twice. After that there was no court left to pay for a tower. The name Halebidu means old capital, or ruined city. The town was renamed for what happened to it.
chunks.source_name: India That Was, The Hoysaleswara Temple Halebidu

chunks.title: Two shrines under one roof
chunks.body: This is a dvikuta vimana: two sanctums side by side, sharing a hall. One is Hoysaleswara, named for the king Vishnuvardhana. The other is Shantaleswara, named for his queen Shantala Devi. Each has its own Nandi pavilion in front, and the two Nandis are different sizes and face their own shrine. An inscription dated 1121 credits the commission to Ketamalla, an officer of the king, with funding from wealthy Shaiva citizens of the town. So a temple named for a king was paid for by his officials and merchants. Walk between the two pavilions and compare the Nandis.
chunks.source_name: India That Was, The Hoysaleswara Temple Halebidu

chunks.title: Walk the wall and count nothing twice
chunks.body: Go round the outside slowly, clockwise, at the level of the wall bands. Elephants at the bottom, then lions, then horses, then foliage, then the epics, then makaras, then swans. There are said to be around two hundred and forty large wall images and thousands of small ones, and the claim is that no two are identical. Test it on the elephants. Pick a stretch of twenty and look at the trunks and the ears. They differ. Then find Ravana lifting Mount Kailasa, and Krishna holding up Govardhan. Those two are the panels to slow down for.
chunks.source_name: Kamat's Potpourri, The Hoysaleswara Temple of Halebidu

chunks.title: Look for the faces that were struck off
chunks.body: On some panels the figures are complete and on others the faces and hands are gone, cleanly, at the same height. That is deliberate damage from the fourteenth-century raids, not weathering. Weathering rounds a whole surface. A chisel takes a face and leaves the drapery beside it sharp. Once you can tell the difference you will read the walls differently: this temple is both a nine-hundred-year-old workshop and a crime scene, and both records are on the same stone. Neither has been cleaned away. Sight along the eye line of a row of figures and the pattern of the damage becomes obvious.
chunks.source_name: Kamat's Potpourri, The Hoysaleswara Temple of Halebidu

chunks.title: The Nandis are polished from touch
chunks.body: Go into each of the two Nandi pavilions. The larger Nandi is over four metres long, monolithic, and its flank is black and glossy where hands have passed over it for centuries. Look at the bell collar and the anklets: the beadwork is cut free of the body with gaps you can see daylight through. Then stand behind the Nandi and look through the doorway at the sanctum beyond. That sightline, bull to god, is why the pavilion is where it is. Everything in the plan is arranged on that axis.

chunks.title: Open all day, lawn all around
chunks.body: This is an Archaeological Survey monument, generally open from about half past six in the morning until half past six in the evening, with no midday closure, so it is the better of the two temples to visit between one and three when Belur shuts its sanctum. Shoes come off at the platform. There is a wide lawn around the temple with shade at the edges, which makes it an easier stop with children or with anyone who needs to sit. Sixteen kilometres from Belur, about half an hour by road.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Halebidu site information

chunks.title: The smaller one nobody walks to
chunks.body: About five minutes from the main temple, past the museum, there is a second Hoysala temple that most visitors never reach. Kedareshwara was built around 1219 by Ketaladevi, a queen of Veera Ballala the Second. It is a trikuta, three shrines, on the same star plan, and the carving is as fine as Hoysaleswara but the site is empty. Because the crowd is not here you can get close to the wall bands and take your time. If Halebidu felt rushed, this is where you recover it. There is no ticket counter and no guide waiting here.
chunks.source_name: India That Was, The Hoysaleswara Temple Halebidu

chunks.title: The pieces that fell off, laid out on grass
chunks.body: This small museum sits on the temple lawn and it holds sculpture recovered from around Halebidu: fragments, hero stones, inscriptions, loose bracket figures. Because these pieces are at eye level and out of the wall you can see the back of the carving and how thin the undercutting really is. That is not possible on the temple itself, where everything is high up and attached. Twenty minutes, small entry fee, usually closed on Fridays. Do it after the temple, not before, so you know what you are looking at. Photography rules vary, so ask at the desk.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Halebidu museum information

chunks.title: Polished black pillars and a mirror floor
chunks.body: A short way from the Hoysaleswara temple there is a group of Jain basadis, twelfth century, from the same dynasty. Go into the Parshvanatha basadi and look at the pillars. They are lathe-turned and polished to a mirror finish, and there is a spot where you can see the ceiling reflected in the stone floor. The carving here is restrained rather than dense, because Jain temples of this period used plainness on purpose. The Hoysalas patronised both faiths at once. Vishnuvardhana himself was born a Jain. Shoes come off at the compound gate, as at the main temple.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Halebidu site notes

chunks.title: A stepwell with twenty-seven shrines around it
chunks.body: About four kilometres from Halebidu there is a Hoysala stepwell called Hulikere Kalyani, and hardly anyone goes. Steps descend on all four sides to the water and small shrine niches are set into the tiers, twenty-seven of them. It was a ritual bathing tank attached to the old capital. There is no ticket, no guard, no signage. Go in the morning when the water is still. The reflection of the shrine niches in the surface is the reason to make the detour. Ask locally for directions; the turning is not marked.

chunks.title: Something for the afternoon after two temples
chunks.body: The Yagachi reservoir is about six kilometres from Belur and it runs boating, jet skis and kayaks. It is not remarkable, but two Hoysala temples in one day is a lot of concentration and this is a reasonable place to let it go, especially with teenagers. Late afternoon is best, the water is calmer and the light on the hills behind is good. Life jackets are provided. Check whether operations are running in the monsoon months, because they suspend when the reservoir is high. Rates are per activity rather than per hour, so ask before you sign anything.

chunks.title: Belur first or Halebidu first
chunks.body: Do Belur in the morning and Halebidu after lunch. Two reasons. Belur closes its sanctum in the middle of the day and Halebidu does not, so the timings fit. And Belur is the denser, more demanding building, so take it while you are fresh. The two are sixteen kilometres apart, about thirty minutes. From Chikmagalur town it is roughly an hour to Belur. From Hassan it is about forty minutes. Budget two hours at Belur and ninety minutes at Halebidu including the museum, and do not try to add Somanathapura on the same day.

chunks.title: Shantala Devi, dancer and queen
chunks.body: Vishnuvardhana's queen Shantala Devi was a trained dancer and a patron of the arts, and she is woven through these buildings. The second sanctum at Halebidu is named for her. Tradition says she modelled for the Darpana Sundari at Belur. Inscriptions record her gifts to temples in her own name, which was not routine. She was a Jain by birth in a court that turned to Vaishnavism, and both traditions were funded side by side while she lived. When you look at the dancing brackets, remember that the queen who may have posed for them knew the technique from the inside.

chunks.title: How to read a Hoysala wall in five minutes
chunks.body: Work from the ground up. The bottom band is elephants, for strength and for the foundation. Above them lions, for courage. Above them horses, for speed. Then a band of foliage and scrollwork. Then the narrative band, scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata. Then makaras, the water creatures. Then hamsas, the swans, at the top. Above all that, the large figures of gods in their niches. Once you have the order, any Hoysala temple opens up, at Belur, at Halebidu or at Somanathapura near Mysuru. Start at the north-east corner and work clockwise.
chunks.source_name: UNESCO Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas listing, general reference

chunks.title: Look for the panel that is two animals
chunks.body: Somewhere on the Halebidu wall there is a carving that reads as a bull from one side and an elephant from the other, using the same block of stone and the same lines. There are several of these puzzle carvings across the Hoysala temples. A guide will walk you straight to them. They exist because the sculptors were showing off inside a very tight brief, and because a viewer walking round the building at a fixed distance passes each panel at a changing angle. The building assumes you are moving. The carvings are built for that.

chunks.title: The erotic panels, and where they sit
chunks.body: There are erotic carvings on these temples and they are usually on the lower bands, near the base, not on the main figures above. Guides sometimes skip them and sometimes make a performance of them. Neither is necessary. In Hoysala practice these belong to the register of worldly life, which sits literally below the register of the gods. The building is arranged as a climb: the material world at your knee, the epics at your chest, the deities at your eye and above. The placement is the argument. Nobody who worships here treats them as scandalous.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Hoysala site notes

chunks.title: Talakad, 1116, and why Belur exists
chunks.body: Vishnuvardhana beat the Cholas at Talakad on the Kaveri in 1116. Belur was consecrated the following year to mark it. That is the direct line: a battle in one place produces a temple in another. It also produced a change of faith. Vishnuvardhana was born a Jain and moved to Vaishnavism under the teacher Ramanuja, and the Chennakeshava temple is a Vaishnava building. So the temple is three things at once: a war memorial, a conversion statement, and a hundred-year employment scheme for the best stone carvers in the Deccan.

chunks.title: Dakshina Varanasi, and what the name is doing
chunks.body: Belur is sometimes called Dakshina Varanasi, the Varanasi of the south. That is a claim, not a description. Calling a town a southern Varanasi is a way of borrowing status from the north, and towns across India have done it. What Belur actually has is different from Varanasi: not a river ghat culture but a single extraordinary building and a temple economy around it. Take the nickname as evidence of ambition. The Hoysalas were a regional dynasty that wanted to be read as a great one, and their buildings argue the case better than the nickname does.

chunks.title: Filter coffee is the drink between temples
chunks.body: You are in coffee country now, and the right thing to drink between Belur and Halebidu is a filter coffee. It comes in a steel tumbler sitting in a wider steel bowl. You pour it back and forth between the two to cool it and to raise the froth. Do it from a height. Drink it from the bowl, not the tumbler, unless you like burnt lips. It will be sweet and milky unless you ask otherwise. Ask for less sugar if you want to taste the roast, and expect to be looked at oddly for it.

chunks.title: Akki rotti and the plate around it
chunks.body: In the small eating houses of this belt, look for akki rotti: a flat rice-flour bread, patted out by hand with onion, coriander and green chilli worked into the dough, cooked on a griddle. It comes with coconut chutney or a spoon of butter. It is a breakfast dish and it goes by mid-morning. Alongside it you may see ragi mudde, a stiff ball of finger millet eaten with a thin curry. You do not chew mudde. You break a piece, dip it, swallow it. Say so if you have never tried it and someone will show you.

chunks.title: Nine hundred years, and the roof is still off
chunks.body: Here is a thing to hold as you leave. Halebidu has stood for nine hundred years without the tower it was designed for. Belur took a century to build and then had a foreign gopura bolted to its front. Somanathapura was finished and then abandoned. Not one of these buildings is in the state its makers intended. They are the best stone carving in south India and every one of them is a compromise with history. That is not a sad ending. It is what survives when a small dynasty spends everything it has on stone.

chunks.title: Where the Hoysalas came from
chunks.body: They started in the hills, at Sosevur in the Western Ghats, as feudatories of the Western Chalukyas. Through the eleventh and twelfth centuries they took their independence and pushed down onto the plains, first with Belur as capital, then Halebidu. At their height they held most of what is now Karnataka and parts of Tamil Nadu. The dynasty ended in the fourteenth century after the Delhi raids, and the ground they lost was picked up by two brothers who founded a city on the Tungabhadra in 1336. Hoysala to Vijayanagara is a direct handover.

chunks.title: Stand at the corner of the platform at Belur
chunks.body: Before you leave Belur, go to a corner of the raised platform, where two arms of the star meet, and crouch a little so your eye is at the level of the wall bands. From there you are looking along the surface rather than at it, and the undercutting suddenly shows: how far each figure stands off the wall, how deep the shadows go, how little stone is actually holding them on. From straight ahead, it is decoration. From the corner, it is engineering. Do this once and you will do it at every Hoysala temple after.

chunks.title: Getting here without a car
chunks.body: Belur and Halebidu are not on a railway. The nearest useful station is Hassan, about forty minutes from Belur, with trains from Bengaluru and Mysuru. From Hassan bus stand there are frequent state buses to Belur and less frequent ones to Halebidu, and a shared auto or taxi between the two temples is straightforward. If you are coming from Chikmagalur town, buses run but they are slow. Hiring a car for the day from Hassan or Chikmagalur is the practical answer and is not expensive split between three or four people.

chunks.title: The lamp that shows you the ceiling
chunks.body: Inside these temples the ceilings are worked in deep concentric bands with a pendant boss hanging at the centre, and the halls are dark. Guides carry a lamp or a torch and hold it up so the carving comes out of the gloom. If you are alone, use your phone light, held low and to one side rather than straight up. Sideways light gives you the depth. Flat light from directly below flattens everything. This is the same rule as the outside walls in the morning sun, applied indoors. Turn your light off between panels and let your eyes rest.

chunks.title: The inscriptions are a payroll
chunks.body: Hoysala temples carry inscriptions in old Kannada on the platform, on the walls and on the pillars, and a lot of them are not prayers. They are grants: this village's revenue assigned to this temple, this much oil for these lamps, this much land to feed these many priests. Read a translation panel if there is one. What you get is the running cost of a twelfth-century temple, written on the temple, in public, so that nobody could quietly stop paying. That is why they survive when the account books do not.

chunks.title: The town of boiled beans
chunks.body: A Hoysala king, Veera Ballala, was lost and hungry in the forest here. He came to a hut and an old woman gave him a bowl of boiled beans. When he founded a settlement on the spot he called it Bendakaaluru, the town of boiled beans. That is the story every child in this city is told. Historians point at an older stone inscription that already carries a version of the name, so the king may have found the name rather than made it. Either way, a city that now runs on software is named after a meal somebody gave away for nothing.
chunks.source_name: IOL Travel, The town of boiled beans

chunks.title: Kempegowda laid out four roads and a mud fort
chunks.body: In 1537 a chieftain from Magadi named Kempe Gowda built a mud fort here and laid out a town inside it. He set two main streets crossing at right angles, Chikkapete running east to west and Doddapete north to south, and he assigned trades to each quarter. Those quarters still carry their trade names: Balepet for bangles, Akkipet for rice, Taragupet for grain, Cottonpet for cotton. Walk the old town today and the street plan is still his. A city that has been rebuilt four times over has kept the grid of a sixteenth-century market.
chunks.source_name: IOL Travel, The town of boiled beans

chunks.title: Four towers, and a wife who paid for them
chunks.body: Kempegowda's successor built four stone watchtowers to mark the limits the city should not grow beyond. They stand at Lalbagh, at Kempambudhi lake, near Ulsoor lake, and at Mekhri Circle. The city passed all four of them centuries ago. There is a story attached to the older fort too: that the walls kept collapsing until Kempegowda's daughter-in-law Lakshmi Devi gave her own life at the south gate to make them stand. A memorial to her is at the Koramangala side. Take the story as a story. The towers are real and you can walk to all four in a day.

chunks.title: A sultan's garden that became a science project
chunks.body: Hyder Ali laid this out in 1760 as a formal Mughal-style pleasure garden. His son Tipu Sultan carried it on and imported plants from Persia, Afghanistan, Mauritius, Turkey and France. After 1799 the British kept it, and in the nineteenth century it turned into a working botanical garden with a herbarium and plant introduction programmes. So its history runs sultan, then coloniser, then state department, and each one added a layer. Two hundred and forty acres, over eighteen hundred species. It is one of the oldest botanical gardens in India and it is still doing research.

chunks.title: Climb the rock, it is three billion years old
chunks.body: There is a bare grey dome of rock inside Lalbagh with one of Kempegowda's towers on top. That is peninsular gneiss and it is around three billion years old, one of the oldest rock formations on the planet. It has been declared a national geological monument. Climb it in the early morning. It takes five minutes, the surface is grippy, and from the top you get the garden below and the city beyond it. Go before eight. After that the rock is hot and the light is flat. Wear shoes with some grip, because the surface is polished smooth in places.
chunks.source_name: Geological Survey of India, national geological monuments

chunks.title: The Glass House and the two flower shows
chunks.body: The Glass House in the middle of Lalbagh was built in 1889, modelled on the Crystal Palace in London, and it holds two flower shows a year: one around Republic Day in January and one around Independence Day in August. Those weeks the garden is packed and the entry queue runs down the road. Outside them the Glass House is quiet and mostly empty. Gates open early, around six, and the garden is at its best in that first hour when the walking clubs are out and the lake has mist on it.

chunks.title: Two storeys of teak in the middle of a market
chunks.body: This is a small two-storey building of teak pillars and arches, finished in 1791, and Tipu called it Rashk-e-Jannat, the envy of heaven. It sits now surrounded by the traffic and shops of the old city, which makes the scale of it surprising. Look at the pillars. They are wood, painted, and they carry the whole upper floor with no masonry columns. Traces of the original floral painting survive on the ceilings and in the corner rooms. It takes twenty minutes. It is one of the few pre-colonial buildings left in central Bengaluru.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Tipu Sultan's Palace Bangalore

chunks.title: Stand on the upper balcony and think about 1791
chunks.body: Go up to the first floor and stand at the balcony. Tipu held court here. The same year the palace was finished, Lord Cornwallis stormed Bangalore fort a few hundred metres from where you are standing. Tipu lost the city and got it back by treaty. Eight years later he was dead at Srirangapatna. This little wooden building is the surviving furniture of a war that decided who would rule south India. Look down at the garden, then out at the market beyond it, and hold both. The market noise below has not changed much either.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Tipu Sultan's Palace Bangalore

chunks.title: What is left of the mud fort
chunks.body: Kempegowda's fort was mud. Hyder Ali rebuilt it in stone in 1761. Cornwallis breached it in 1791 and the British later pulled most of it down to lay out the city. What survives is one gate, the Delhi Gate, and a short stretch of wall with two bastions, wedged next to a hospital and a market. Go and look at the breach point, which is marked. It is not much. But it is the only piece of the defensive city left, and standing in it explains why the streets around here bend the way they do.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Bangalore Fort

chunks.title: The bull that kept eating the groundnuts
chunks.body: The story here is agricultural. Farmers on this land kept losing their groundnut crop to a bull that came at night. They set a watch, and when the bull appeared they struck it, and it sat down and turned to stone. So they built a temple around it, and every year since they have brought the first groundnut harvest to it as an offering. That is the origin of the Kadalekai Parishe. The temple around the bull was built by Kempegowda in the sixteenth century. The stone bull is nearly five metres high.

chunks.title: The groundnut fair, on the last Monday of Karthika
chunks.body: Kadalekai Parishe fills the streets around this temple for two or three days each year. Farmers bring the first groundnut crop and pile it in heaps: raw, boiled, roasted, in the shell and out. Alongside them come bangle sellers, clay toys, sugar candies and fried snacks. It is held on the last Monday of the month of Karthika, so the English date moves each year, usually falling in November or December. Over two hundred groundnut vendors trade. If you are in the city that week, go in the evening. Ask locally for the exact date before you plan around it.

chunks.title: The bull is oiled and it is growing
chunks.body: Walk right round the Nandi inside. The granite is black and slick with oil and charcoal, rubbed on for centuries. There is a local claim that the statue has grown over time and that a trident was fixed on its head to stop it. That is a story. What is true is that the stone was carved in place from a boulder already on this rock outcrop, the same peninsular gneiss you can see at Lalbagh and at Bugle Rock next door. The temple was built around it afterwards. The trident is certainly there. The growth has never been measured.

chunks.title: Butter, one hundred kilos of it
chunks.body: Next to the Bull Temple is a large Ganesha, about five and a half metres, also carved from the rock. On certain days he is covered in butter, up to a hundred kilograms of it, packed over the whole surface. It is called benne alankara. After some days the butter is taken off and distributed. Go and look on a butter day if you can; the figure becomes pale yellow and completely smooth. On other days you see the plain stone and the difference is startling. Ask at the temple which is on.

chunks.title: Built to answer a remark
chunks.body: This is the state legislature, finished in 1956, granite, four storeys, with a dome and a lot of columns. The story attached is that Kengal Hanumanthaiah, then chief minister, was stung by a visitor's remark that Bangalore's public buildings looked too European, and set out to build something in an Indian idiom at a scale nobody could ignore. Over the entrance is the line: Government Work is God's Work. You cannot go inside without permission. Come at night when it is floodlit, which happens on Sundays and public holidays, and look at it from the Cubbon Park side.
chunks.source_name: Government of Karnataka, Vidhana Soudha, general reference

chunks.title: Three hundred acres the city keeps arguing about
chunks.body: Cubbon Park was laid out in 1870 and it sits right in the middle of the city, about three hundred acres of trees, paths and old red buildings. Roads run through it and there is a long-running fight about closing them to traffic. On Sundays some roads shut and the park fills with walkers, dogs, cyclists and readers. That is the day to come. Find the Attara Kacheri, the red brick High Court building, and the bandstand. The tree cover here is one of the reasons this city stayed cool for so long.
chunks.source_name: Horticulture Department, Government of Karnataka, general reference

chunks.title: Sit under a rain tree for twenty minutes
chunks.body: Find one of the big spreading rain trees, put your back against it and stay for twenty minutes. Bengaluru is loud and this is one of the few places in the centre where the traffic drops behind the trees. Listen for the coppersmith barbet, a flat repeated tok tok tok that sounds like someone hammering metal a long way off. You will hear it before you find it. Early morning and just before dusk are when the park works. In the middle of a weekday it is a shortcut for office traffic.

chunks.title: A Tudor house in the tropics
chunks.body: This was built in 1878 for a British guardian of the Mysore royal minor, then bought by the Wadiyars. The design borrows from Windsor Castle: battlements, turrets, fortified towers, and inside, timber panelling, Gothic windows and a ballroom. It is still owned by the Mysore royal family, which is why the ticket is expensive and the audio guide is included. The grounds are used for concerts. Whether it is worth the price depends on your appetite for nineteenth-century pastiche, but the wooden interiors are genuinely good. Check the concert calendar first, because the grounds close for events.
chunks.source_name: Bangalore Palace heritage records, general reference

chunks.title: Older than the city that grew around it
chunks.body: This temple at Halasuru is Chola in origin, older than Kempegowda's town, and it was extended under Vijayanagara. That makes it one of the oldest working buildings in Bengaluru. The gopura and the pillared hall are Vijayanagara work, with yali pillars and a well-carved kalyana mandapa. Look for the panels of Shiva and Parvati on the outer wall. It is in a busy neighbourhood and easy to walk past. Ten minutes inside, and it resets your sense of how old this city actually is. Go in the morning, when the hall is open and the street outside is still quiet.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Someshwara Temple Halasuru

chunks.title: A tank from the sixteenth century with islands in it
chunks.body: Ulsoor is one of the older tanks in the city, associated with Kempegowda and later reworked. It has islands, a walking path and boating. Like all of Bengaluru's lakes it is a made thing: this was a dry plateau with no big river, so every settlement dug tanks and chained them together so overflow from one fed the next. That chain is why places are called kere and why so many neighbourhoods are named after water that is no longer there. Walk the bund in the early morning. One of Kempegowda's four towers stands nearby.

chunks.title: Named for the engineer who dug it
chunks.body: Sankey Tank was built in 1882 by Colonel Richard Sankey, chief engineer of Mysore, to supply water to the growing town. It is now a walking lake with a path around it, ducks, and a lot of people doing laps at six in the morning. The point of coming is not the lake, it is the hour. Bengaluru at dawn is a different city: cool, quiet, smelling of wet earth and coffee. Do one circuit, then walk five minutes into Malleshwaram for breakfast. That sequence is the best morning this city offers.

chunks.title: The masala dosa they have made since 1943
chunks.body: Vidyarthi Bhavan opened in 1943 to feed students in Basavanagudi. The dish is the masala dosa: deep red-brown, crisp, thick with ghee, folded over a potato filling, served with coconut chutney and no sambar unless you ask. There will be a queue on the pavement. You share a table with strangers. The waiters carry six plates on one arm and will not take an order twice. Order two dosas and a coffee. Do not ask for changes to the dish. That is not rudeness on their part, it is that there is only one dish.

chunks.title: Rava idli was invented during a rice shortage
chunks.body: MTR started in 1924. During the Second World War rice was rationed and short, so the kitchen substituted semolina and steamed it, and rava idli came out of the shortage. It is now standard across south India. Come here for that, and for the thali, which arrives in courses with staff refilling until you stop them. At the end you get a filter coffee. There is a queue at peak times and they give you a token. Breakfast finishes and the kitchen closes between services, so check the hours before you walk over.

chunks.title: Benne masala dosa, and what benne means
chunks.body: Benne is butter. At CTR in Malleshwaram the dosa is cooked in it, finished with more of it, and arrives glistening. It is smaller and softer than the Vidyarthi Bhavan version and there is more of the butter and less of the crunch. Get there before nine on a weekday or expect to wait. Order a benne masala dosa and, if you can still manage it, a plate of idli vada. Eat, pay, leave; the tables turn fast and lingering is not the culture here. Malleshwaram's Eighth Cross is worth a walk afterwards.

chunks.title: Flowers by the tonne, before six in the morning
chunks.body: This is the wholesale flower market and it works at night. Between about three and six in the morning, tonnes of roses, marigolds, jasmine and chrysanthemum come in from farms across the district and are sold by weight in gunny sacks. By eight it is a retail market and the volume has gone. If you want the real thing, come at five with someone who knows the way in. It is crowded, wet underfoot, and physically hard going. It sits on the ground where the battle for Bangalore was fought in 1791.

chunks.title: Not the place for a leisurely stroll
chunks.body: Be honest with yourself about this one. KR Market is a working wholesale market with lorries reversing, porters carrying loads at head height, narrow wet lanes and no space to stand still. It is not suitable for anyone unsteady on their feet, and it is not a good first stop with small children. Go early, carry nothing loose, wear shoes you do not mind ruining, and keep to the edges. If someone in your party cannot manage it, Malleshwaram market or the flower rows at Gandhi Bazaar give you the same thing at a tenth of the intensity.

chunks.title: Bargain in the lanes, not the shops
chunks.body: Commercial Street is a hundred and fifty years old as a shopping district and it is now a mix of proper shops, street stalls and lanes going off both sides. The rule is simple: prices in the fixed shops are fixed, prices on the street are not. Start at about half in the lanes and settle around sixty percent. Go on a weekday morning. Weekend evenings are shoulder to shoulder. Parking is impossible; take the metro to a nearby station and walk. The side lanes towards Ibrahim Sahib Street are where the older trade is.

chunks.title: The bookshops are the reason to walk it
chunks.body: Church Street was repaved as a pedestrian-friendly street and it holds the last of the city's old bookshops alongside the newer cafes and bars. Blossom Book House runs over several floors of secondhand stock and people lose afternoons in it. Around the corner, MG Road has the Metro overhead now where the promenade used to be. Come in the evening. This is where Bengaluru's reputation as a going-out city actually shows itself, and it is walkable, which very little of this city is. Weekend evenings are closed to traffic, which is when the street is at its best.

chunks.title: A temple built like an airport
chunks.body: This opened in 1997 and it is designed to move very large numbers of people through a fixed route: ramps, queue rails, a long approach, shops on the way out. On a festival day it handles crowds in the tens of thousands. Whatever you think of the architecture, watch the crowd management, because it is the most efficient religious logistics in the city. Go on a weekday morning if you want to see the shrines without the press. There is a free meal service and a large prasadam counter. Shoes and phones go into lockers at the entrance.

chunks.title: Named for the engineer who built the dam
chunks.body: This museum is named for M. Visvesvaraya, the engineer behind the Krishna Raja Sagara dam at Mysuru and later Diwan of Mysore. It opened in 1962 and it is hands-on: engines you can crank, a working Wright Flyer replica, an electronics gallery, a dinosaur enclosure that children go straight to. It is the right stop in this city for a wet afternoon or a restless ten-year-old. Allow two hours. It sits next to Cubbon Park, so it pairs well with the park and the gallery next door. Tickets are sold at the gate and the queue moves quickly.
chunks.source_name: National Council of Science Museums, general reference

chunks.poi: National Gallery of Modern Art, Bengaluru
chunks.title: A colonial house with Ravi Varma upstairs
chunks.body: The gallery is in Manikyavelu Mansion, an early twentieth-century house on Palace Road, and the collection runs from the colonial period to contemporary Indian art. There are Raja Ravi Varma works here, and Amrita Sher-Gil, and Jamini Roy. The old house and the new wing are joined, so you walk from panelled rooms into white gallery space. Closed Mondays. It is quiet, it is air-conditioned, and the garden has old trees. Give it ninety minutes and start upstairs in the old building where the earlier work hangs. Bags go into a cloakroom at the entrance.
chunks.source_name: National Gallery of Modern Art, Bengaluru, general reference

chunks.title: Sit in the cockpit of a fighter
chunks.body: Hindustan Aeronautics has been building aircraft in this city since 1940, and this museum on the Old Airport Road holds their history: HF-24 Marut, MiG-21, Kiran, Ajeet, helicopters, and a simulator you can sit in. Several aircraft are open so you can climb into the cockpit. There is also a hall on the history of Indian aviation and the story of how HAL came to be here at all. Closed Mondays. It is the best answer in Bengaluru to a child who has had enough of temples and gardens. Photography is allowed in the outdoor yard.
chunks.source_name: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited museum records, general reference

chunks.title: Tipu's summer fort above the clouds
chunks.body: Sixty kilometres north of the city, this hill rises to about fourteen hundred and seventy metres and Tipu Sultan used it as a summer retreat. His small palace is still there, and so is a cliff called Tipu's Drop with a long fall below it. There is a Chola-period Bhoganandeeshwara temple at the base of the hill that is older than everything above. Between November and February the valley below fills with cloud at dawn and you look down on it. That is what people come for. The temple at the base of the hill is free to enter.
chunks.source_name: Karnataka Tourism, Nandi Hills, general reference

chunks.title: Leave at four in the morning or do not bother
chunks.body: For the cloud view you have to be at the top before sunrise, which means leaving central Bengaluru around four. Gates usually open at six but the road up can queue badly on weekends and entry is sometimes capped. Go on a weekday. The road has forty hairpins and is not comfortable for anyone prone to travel sickness. It is cold at the top before dawn, genuinely cold by Bengaluru standards, so carry a layer. If you cannot face four in the morning, skip it: at ten it is an ordinary hill with a crowd.

chunks.title: The safari is a bus, and that is the point
chunks.body: Bannerghatta has a zoo, a butterfly park and a safari where you go through fenced enclosures in a bus: herbivores, then tigers, then lions, then bears. It is not a wilderness and it does not pretend to be. Book the safari slot ahead online, especially at weekends, because the tickets go. Go for the first safari of the day when the animals are moving. Allow half a day including the drive out, which is about an hour from the centre and longer in traffic. Closed Tuesdays. Carry the booking confirmation on your phone and on paper.

chunks.title: Why this city was cool, and why it is less so
chunks.body: Bengaluru sits at about nine hundred metres, on a plateau, with no river of its own. That altitude is why the British moved the Mysore cantonment here and why it was called an air-conditioned city. Two things have eaten into it. The tank system that once chained hundreds of lakes together has been built over, and the tree cover has thinned. The temperature record shows the change. When people here talk about the old weather they are not being sentimental; there is a measurable difference and it maps onto what happened to the lakes.
chunks.source_name: Indian Institute of Science urban ecology studies, general reference

chunks.title: Two cities that were stitched together
chunks.body: Bengaluru is two towns joined. There is the pete, Kempegowda's market town, west of the centre, with narrow streets named for trades. And there is the cantonment, laid out by the British after 1809 to the east, with wide roads, churches and English street names. They grew separately, had different administrations and different languages of trade, and were only merged into one municipality in 1949. You can still feel the seam. Walk from Chickpet to MG Road and the street grid, the building line and the shop signs all change.

chunks.title: The one-way system will beat you
chunks.body: Practical warning. Bengaluru's traffic is worse than any estimate you have been given, and the one-way system means the return leg of a journey is often nothing like the outward one. Two things help. Use the Metro where it goes; it is fast, cheap and air-conditioned. And do not plan more than two areas in a day. A morning in Basavanagudi and Lalbagh, then an evening on Church Street, is a full day here. Trying to add Bannerghatta or Nandi Hills on the same day is how people end up spending five hours in a car.

chunks.title: Ask for a by-two coffee
chunks.body: Filter coffee here is decoction and boiled milk, served in a steel tumbler in a wider bowl. If two of you want a small one each, ask for a by-two: one coffee split into two sets. Nobody will think it strange. In a darshini you pay at the counter first, take the receipt to the serving window and eat standing. That is the format across the city and it is fast, cheap and good. If you want it less sweet, say kammi sakkare. If you want strong, say strong; it is the same word.

chunks.title: Where to eat a military hotel meal
chunks.body: Look for places calling themselves military hotels. The name goes back to eating houses that served meat when most restaurants in the city were strictly vegetarian. What you get is donne biryani served in a stitched leaf bowl, ragi mudde with a mutton curry, and a boti or liver fry if you want it. Order the mudde if you have never had it: a stiff ball of finger millet, broken and swallowed with the curry rather than chewed. These places are busy at lunch and closed by early evening. Ask for the mutton pulao if the biryani has already gone.

chunks.title: The old lake chain, and the names it left behind
chunks.body: Look at a map and count the place names ending in kere or containing halli. Kere is a tank. Bengaluru had hundreds of them, dug over centuries and connected so that overflow from an upper tank ran into the next one down. That system watered the city on a plateau with no river. Most of the tanks were filled in during the twentieth century and built on: a bus station here, a stadium there, a whole neighbourhood on another. When the city floods now it usually floods along the old chain, because water still knows where the lakes were.
chunks.source_name: Indian Institute of Science urban ecology studies, general reference

chunks.title: Seven beans in a beard
chunks.body: In the seventeenth century a Sufi named Baba Budan came back from Mecca through the Yemeni port of Mocha. Coffee left that port roasted, so that nobody outside Arabia could grow it. He took seven green beans and hid them in his beard. Seven, because seven is a sacred number. He planted them on the slopes above where you are standing. Every coffee estate in India traces back to that. The hills are named for him now: Baba Budangiri. Whether it happened exactly that way is another matter. The coffee is here, and it started somewhere.

chunks.title: A cave two faiths both claim
chunks.body: The shrine here is a cave, and it is contested in a way that matters. Hindus hold it as the seat of Dattatreya. Muslims hold it as the dargah of Baba Budan, and it was administered for centuries by a Muslim custodian while both communities came. Since the 1990s it has been the subject of court cases and political campaigns. Go quietly. The point of the place, historically, is that it was shared for four hundred years, and that shared use is the older tradition, older than the argument about it.

chunks.title: The highest ground in Karnataka
chunks.body: At around nineteen hundred and thirty metres, this is the highest point in the state, part of the Chandra Drona range of the Western Ghats. The name comes from a small Mullappa Swamy shrine at the summit. There is a road most of the way and then a set of steps with a handrail to the top, a few hundred of them. In the monsoon the summit is inside cloud and you will see nothing. From December to February the mornings are clear and cold, and the ridgelines run away from you in layers.

chunks.title: The road up is narrower than your car
chunks.body: The last stretch of road to the Mullayanagiri base is single track with drops on one side and no barrier, and it is used in both directions. If you are not confident, hire a local driver rather than driving yourself. There is limited parking at the base and it fills by mid-morning at weekends. From the parking to the summit is a climb of a few hundred steps with a rail. Wind at the top is strong and constant. This is a poor choice for anyone with mobility trouble or a fear of heights.

chunks.title: The coffee grows in the shade, on purpose
chunks.body: Walk into an estate and look up before you look down. Indian coffee is grown under a canopy of silver oak and native trees, with pepper vines climbing the trunks. That shade slows the cherry down and it is why the cup tastes the way it does. It also means an estate is a working forest, so you will see hornbills and langurs while you walk. Robusta sits lower and hotter, arabica higher and cooler. Ask which block you are in. The plants look different once you know what to look for.
chunks.source_name: Coffee Board of India, general reference

chunks.title: Time your visit to the harvest
chunks.body: Flowering happens after the first rains, usually March or April, and for a few days the estates are covered in white blossom and the smell carries for kilometres. Harvest runs roughly November to February, when the cherries turn red and the drying yards are full. Between May and September it rains hard and the estate walks are muddy and leech-ridden. If you want to see coffee being made rather than coffee growing, come in December or January and ask the estate whether they are pulping that week. Estates need notice, so call ahead rather than turning up at the gate.
chunks.source_name: Coffee Board of India, general reference

chunks.title: From cherry to cup, in one room
chunks.body: This small museum lays out the whole chain: the plant, the cherry, pulping, fermenting, drying, hulling, grading, roasting, brewing. If you have walked an estate first, this is where it clicks together. There is usually a tasting and a shop selling estate lots you cannot easily get elsewhere. Ask them to explain the difference between washed and natural processing and then taste both. Half an hour, small entry fee. Do it on the way out of town rather than on the way in. Buy the beans whole rather than ground, because they keep their character for weeks longer.
chunks.source_name: Coffee Board of India, general reference

chunks.title: You cannot drive to it, and that is the deal
chunks.body: Hebbe drops in two stages through an estate below Kemmangundi. You leave your own vehicle and take a forest department jeep for the last several kilometres, over a track that is genuinely rough, and then walk the final stretch through water. There is a queue for the jeeps at weekends. Do not attempt the track in a private car; people try and people get stuck. In the monsoon the flow is heavy and access is sometimes closed. Wear something you can walk in wet and carry your phone in a bag.

chunks.title: The rose garden a maharaja put on a ridge
chunks.body: Kemmangundi was the summer retreat of Krishnaraja Wodeyar the Fourth, and it is sometimes called KR Hills for him. There is a terraced rose garden on the ridge and a viewpoint called Z Point reached by a walk of about a kilometre and a half from the garden. Go for the sunset from Z Point. The walk is gentle but the last part is exposed. The state runs basic accommodation here. It is a good base if you want to do Hebbe Falls and Mullayanagiri without long drives from town.

chunks.title: Ten minutes from town, and empty at six
chunks.body: This is an irrigation lake about ten kilometres from Chikmagalur town, ringed by hills, with a road along the bund. There is nothing to do here, which is why it is worth going. Come at six in the evening, park, and walk the bund. The hills go dark before the water does and the reflection holds the last light for a while. There are no facilities, no stalls and no lighting, so leave before it is properly dark. It is the easiest good half hour in the district. The road round the lake is unlit and narrow.

chunks.title: A tiger reserve most people drive past
chunks.body: Bhadra is a tiger reserve and the Muthodi range is the usual entry point, about forty kilometres from Chikmagalur town. Safaris run morning and evening in forest department vehicles and must be booked; walk-ups are often turned away. You are more likely to see gaur, sambar, elephant and langur than a tiger, and that is the honest expectation to set. Bhadra was the site of one of India's first fully voluntary village relocations out of a protected area, which is why the core is as intact as it is. Book several days ahead in the season.
chunks.source_name: Karnataka Forest Department, Bhadra Tiger Reserve, general reference

chunks.title: Where the town eats breakfast
chunks.body: This is a plain, busy, cheap place in the middle of Chikmagalur town and it is where people actually eat. Order the akki rotti if it is on, or idli vada, and a filter coffee. It fills between eight and ten in the morning and the turnover is fast. Nothing here is presented for visitors, which is the recommendation. If you are heading to Mullayanagiri or Baba Budangiri, eat here first, because there is very little on those roads once you leave town. Expect to share a table, and expect the bill to be smaller than you think.

chunks.title: A thin fall people stand under
chunks.body: Manikyadhara is on the Baba Budangiri road, a narrow fall coming down a rock face, and the tradition is to stand under it. The water is cold and it comes down hard enough to sting. There are stalls at the top selling tea, bhutta and cheap towels, which tells you what everyone does. It is a short walk down steps from the road and a harder walk back up. Combine it with the Dattatreya Peetha cave, which is a few kilometres further on the same road. Change into dry clothes before the drive back up.

chunks.title: White water, and the name it earned
chunks.body: Jhari is called Buttermilk Falls because the water breaks up as it comes down and goes white. It sits below Baba Budangiri and the last stretch is a rough track where local jeeps ferry people from a parking point. Do not take a small car down. The pool at the bottom is shallow and people sit in it. In the dry months, March to May, the flow drops to very little and it is not worth the trip. Go between July and January when there is water. There are no changing facilities at the bottom.

chunks.title: A river starts in a tank the size of a room
chunks.body: The Kaveri feeds a large part of south India, waters two states and has been fought over in court for a century. It starts here, in a small stone tank on the side of Brahmagiri hill, a hole called the Brahmakundike. You can walk round the tank in twenty seconds. On the day of Tula Sankramana in October, usually the seventeenth, water is said to well up in the spring at a fixed moment and thousands come to see it. Stand at the tank and try to hold both facts: this cup of water, and the river it becomes.

chunks.title: Climb the steps behind the tank
chunks.body: Behind the temple tank there is a flight of about four hundred steps up the ridge. Go up. From the top you get the Brahmagiri range on one side and, on a clear day in the dry season, a long view west towards the coastal plain. It is less than a hundred kilometres from here to the Arabian Sea. In the monsoon this whole place is inside cloud and there is no view at all, only rain and a lot of pilgrims. Carry a layer; it is cold and windy at the top even in April.

chunks.title: Three rivers meet before you go up the hill
chunks.body: Bhagamandala is where the Kaveri meets the Kannike and the Sujyoti, a confluence called Triveni Sangama, and pilgrims bathe here before going up to Talakaveri. The temple complex is in the Kerala style, with sloping tiled roofs and copper plating rather than the tall stone towers you see further east. That architecture is the clue to where you are: this is the western edge of Karnataka, and the building traditions of the Malabar coast come over the ghats. Do Bhagamandala first, then Talakaveri. That is the order pilgrims use. Shoes come off at the temple gate.

chunks.title: The Kodavas keep their guns and their ancestors
chunks.body: The Kodavas are the people of this land and their customs are their own. They are one of very few communities in India with a general exemption from the Indian Arms Act, allowed to keep firearms without a licence, because of their martial history. Their weddings have no priest; the elders of the family conduct them. Ancestors are honoured directly at the ainmane, the ancestral home, and the festival of Kailpodh in September is when the weapons are cleaned and blessed. If you are invited into an ainmane, that is not a tourist attraction. Take it seriously.

chunks.title: Three festivals that run the Kodava year
chunks.body: Kailpodh in September, when the weapons come out and are cleaned and honoured. Kaveri Sankramana in October, when the goddess of the river is worshipped at Talakaveri and holy water is carried home in bottles. Puttari in November or December, the harvest festival, when the first sheaf of rice is cut at a fixed hour with the whole family present and carried into the house. If you are here in any of those months, ask your host. These are family events, not public ones, and being asked in is a real thing.

chunks.title: A viewpoint a king used, and a sunset everyone else does
chunks.body: This is a small pavilion on a ridge in Madikeri where the Kodagu kings came to watch the sun go down over the hills. It is now a public garden with a toy train and a lot of people doing exactly the same thing. Come at half past five, get a spot on the wall, and watch the valleys fill up. It is crowded and it is still worth it, because the layered ridgelines going west are the defining view of this district. Small entry fee. Go early in the season, not on a long weekend.

chunks.title: Mud, then stone, then a British clock
chunks.body: The fort at Madikeri was first built in mud in the late seventeenth century by Mudduraja, rebuilt in stone by Tipu Sultan, who renamed the town Jaffarabad, and then taken by the British in 1834. Inside there are two mortar elephants, a church from 1855 that is now the district museum, and the old palace building used as government offices. It is a small site and it holds three regimes in one enclosure. The museum is modest; the point is the layering. Closed Mondays. The clock tower and the fort gate are the two things to photograph before you leave.

chunks.title: Hindu kings in Muslim-style tombs
chunks.body: These are the tombs of the Kodagu kings Doddavirarajendra and Lingarajendra, and of a royal priest. Look at the architecture: domes, minarets at the corners, the whole form of an Indo-Islamic tomb. The rulers were Hindu. They chose this vocabulary because it was the prestige style of the Deccan in that period and because their neighbours in Mysore were building the same way. It is a five-minute walk uphill from the road and it is usually quiet. Go in the late afternoon and look back over the town. There is no ticket and no guide.

chunks.title: A temple built to settle a guilty conscience
chunks.body: The story attached to this temple is that Lingarajendra the Second had a Brahmin killed, was troubled by it, and was told to build a temple to Shiva to be free of it. He built this in 1820. The style is a mix again: an Islamic dome and minarets over a Hindu shrine, with a tank in front full of large fish that people feed. Walk round the tank. The building looks like a mosque from the outside and does not pretend otherwise, and nobody in Madikeri finds that odd.

chunks.title: A fall inside a coffee estate
chunks.body: Abbey Falls is on private estate land near Madikeri and you reach it through coffee and cardamom, along a path and down steps to a hanging bridge that faces the fall. You cannot get into the water; the viewing bridge is as close as it goes. In the monsoon and just after, roughly July to October, the flow is heavy and the noise fills the valley. By March it is thin. The steps down and back are the only real effort. Go early in the day before the buses arrive.

chunks.title: A Tibetan settlement in the coffee hills
chunks.body: Tibetan refugees were settled at Bylakuppe from 1961 on land given by the state, and Namdroling was founded in 1963. It is now one of the largest teaching centres of the Nyingma school outside Tibet, with thousands of monks and nuns. The main temple holds three gilded figures around eighteen metres high. Go in the morning when the halls are in use. Remove shoes, do not photograph during prayers, and walk clockwise. There are Tibetan food stalls outside the gate; the momos and thukpa there are the real thing. Entry to the monastery itself is free.

chunks.title: Working elephants, and what the visit actually is
chunks.body: Dubare was a timber camp of the forest department and the elephants here were trained for that work. Some of them still take part in the Mysuru Dasara procession. The visitor programme involves watching feeding and bathing at the river in the morning, roughly nine to eleven. Rides and direct interaction have been reduced over time on welfare grounds. Cross to the camp by boat. Go for the morning session; by afternoon the elephants are away in the forest and there is little to see. Book the boat crossing and the session together at the counter.

chunks.title: An island of bamboo you reach by rope bridge
chunks.body: Nisargadhama is a small island in the Kaveri near Kushalnagar, reached by a hanging bridge, planted with bamboo, sandalwood and teak. There are deer, a rabbit enclosure, boating and treetop huts. It is a gentle, flat, shaded place, which makes it the right stop in Coorg for anyone who cannot manage falls and hill climbs. An hour is enough. Combine it with Bylakuppe, which is fifteen minutes away, and Dubare, which is about twenty, for an easy day without a single steep step. The rope bridge sways, which children like and some adults do not, but there is a road bridge as well.

chunks.title: Rama's arrow, and the Lakshmana Tirtha
chunks.body: The story here is from the Ramayana. Rama and Lakshmana were passing through the Brahmagiri hills and Rama wanted water, so Lakshmana shot an arrow into the hillside and a stream came out. The river below is called the Lakshmana Tirtha for that reason. The fall drops about sixty metres in two stages and there is a Rameshwara temple at the base. It is a walk of about a kilometre and a half from the parking, uphill and stepped. Best in the months after the monsoon. It is at the far south of the district, near the Kerala border, so it is a long drive from Madikeri.

chunks.title: The jeep track is the attraction
chunks.body: Mandalpatti is a ridge about twenty kilometres from Madikeri and the last eight kilometres are a boulder track that only high-clearance jeeps can take. You park at Abbi Falls road and hire a jeep. The ride is rough enough that people hold on and laugh, and that is honestly half of what you are paying for. At the top, grassland ridges roll away in every direction and in the early morning the valleys below hold cloud. It is closed or impassable in heavy rain. Not suitable for a bad back.

chunks.title: A rock slab, and a warning
chunks.body: Chelavara drops over a broad rock face near Cheyyandane village and it is quieter than Abbey or Iruppu because it is harder to find. People climb onto the rock beside and above the fall for photographs. That rock is smooth, it is wet, and there have been deaths here. Look at it from the base. The walk down from the road is short and steep. Go between October and January when there is water and the rock is not being scrambled on by a crowd. There is no railing and no rescue nearby.

chunks.title: Pandi curry, kachampuli and akki roti
chunks.body: The dish to eat here is pandi curry, pork cooked dark and sour. The sourness comes from kachampuli, a thick black vinegar made by reducing the juice of the kokum-like Garcinia fruit. It is not tamarind and it does not taste like it. Eat it with kadambuttu, steamed rice balls, or with akki roti. If you do not eat pork, ask for koli curry, which is chicken done the same way, or the bamboo shoot dish when it is in season. Home-stay kitchens do this far better than restaurants. Ask for the vinegar on the side if you are unsure.

chunks.title: Buy pepper and cardamom where it is graded
chunks.body: Kodagu grows pepper, cardamom and coffee, often on the same land, with the pepper vines climbing the shade trees over the coffee. In the Madikeri market you can buy all three, and the thing to look for is grading. Ask for the grade, not just the price: bold cardamom pods are larger and greener, and pepper is sorted by size and density. Buy small quantities from a shop that will tell you the estate. Wild honey from the forest gatherers is also sold here and is worth a jar. Vacuum packing is usually offered free.

chunks.title: Coorg is a district, not a town
chunks.body: Set expectations before you arrive. Kodagu, which the British called Coorg, is a hill district about the size of a small county, and the things people come for are spread across it. Madikeri is the main town and a reasonable base for the north. Talakaveri and Bhagamandala are about forty minutes west of it. Iruppu and Nagarhole are more than two hours south. Roads are narrow, winding and slow, so thirty kilometres can take an hour. Pick a base and do one direction a day rather than trying to cross the district twice.

chunks.title: When the rain here is the point, and when it is not
chunks.body: Kodagu gets very heavy monsoon rain, June to September, and the district has had serious landslides in recent years, with roads cut for days. That is the season the waterfalls are at their best and the season travel is least reliable. October to February is the settled window: green from the rain, clear, cold in the mornings. March to May is dry and the falls thin out. If you come in the monsoon, keep your plans loose and check road conditions locally rather than online. Homestays book out over long weekends in the clear months.

chunks.title: More people come here than to the Taj Mahal
chunks.body: Here is a number that surprises people. This palace draws visitor figures in the same range as the Taj Mahal, and in some years it has been reported ahead of it. Most of those visitors are Indian, and most of them are from Karnataka. That changes what you are standing in. This is not a monument that foreigners discovered and locals tolerate. It is a place families come to on a Sunday, in their good clothes, with children who have been told the stories on the bus. Look at the crowd around you as much as at the building. The crowd is the point.

chunks.title: The wrestlers train through the night
chunks.body: In the old quarters of this city there are garadi mane, earthen wrestling houses, and men still train in them the way they did when the palace paid for it. The floor is red earth mixed with oil and turmeric, turned over before each session. The Dasara wrestling tournament is the surviving public face of it. If someone offers to take you into a garadi at five in the morning, go. You will see rope climbing, stone weights, and a form of wrestling with rules older than the Wadiyars. Ask before you photograph. These are training halls, not exhibitions.

chunks.title: An entire city was designed as a stage
chunks.body: Look at how wide the roads are here compared with any other Indian city of this age. That is deliberate. Mysuru was laid out under the Wadiyars and their engineers with the Dasara procession in mind: a fixed route from the palace to the Bannimantap parade ground, wide enough for elephants and crowds, with sightlines to the palace and the hill. The lakes, the parks and the public buildings were placed around it. You are walking through a piece of nineteenth-century urban planning built to hold one ten-day event, and it holds the rest of the year as a side effect.
chunks.source_name: Mysuru city planning history, general reference

chunks.title: The city ran on electricity before most of Europe
chunks.body: In 1905 Mysuru became one of the first cities in Asia to get street lighting from hydroelectric power, drawn from the Shivanasamudra falls on the Kaveri about a hundred kilometres away. The transmission line was among the longest in the world at the time. The Maharaja lit the palace with it, which is where the illumination tradition you see on Sundays begins. So the bulbs on the palace are not a modern tourist display bolted on later. They are the surviving habit of a state that treated electricity as a public statement.
chunks.source_name: Kaveri hydroelectric scheme records, general reference

chunks.title: The steps have numbers, and people paint them
chunks.body: As you climb, look down at the stone. Many of the steps carry a number, and many carry smears of vermilion and turmeric left by people who stopped there. Pilgrims apply it as they go, so the higher you get the more worn and layered the colour becomes. Some climbers count aloud. Others stop at every hundredth step to rest and to mark it. The practice is not organised by anyone. It has simply accumulated. Watch where people put their hands and their offerings and you will learn the etiquette of this climb faster than anyone can explain it.

chunks.title: Rome, and a city nobody in Europe believed
chunks.body: When Domingo Paes wrote that this place was as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world, readers in Portugal treated it as traveller's exaggeration. It was not. Modern survey work puts the fortified urban area at something over twenty-five square kilometres, with a population estimated in the hundreds of thousands, fed by a canal system that is still being mapped. Stand anywhere here and turn a full circle. What you can see in every direction, boulder to boulder, was inside the walls of one city. Then remember it took five months to break.
chunks.source_name: BA Notes, Paes and Nuniz on Vijayanagara

chunks.title: Colin Mackenzie found it, in a way
chunks.body: After 1565 this place was known locally and ignored elsewhere. In 1799, the same year Tipu died, a Scottish surveyor named Colin Mackenzie came through and made the first systematic drawings and notes of the ruins. He collected inscriptions, hired local scholars to read them, and sent the material to Calcutta. That is where the modern archaeological record of Vijayanagara begins. The people living here had never forgotten what it was. What Mackenzie did was write it down in a language the rest of the world would read, which is a different thing from finding it.
chunks.source_name: Mackenzie Collection, British Library, general reference

chunks.title: The city was watered by hand-cut stone channels
chunks.body: Look for the low stone gutters running across the ground, sometimes cut straight into bedrock, sometimes carried on short aqueducts. Those are the arteries. Water was taken from the Tungabhadra upstream, run through channels along contour lines, and fed to tanks, baths, fields and the palace enclosure. Some of those channels are still delivering water to farmers today, five hundred years after the court that dug them was destroyed. Once you start noticing them you cannot stop. The temples are what people photograph. The channels are what made a city possible in a place with no soil and no shade.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Vijayanagara research reports

chunks.title: Horses were the empire's great weakness
chunks.body: Vijayanagara could not breed good warhorses. The climate and the grazing were wrong. So it bought them, thousands a year, from Arabia and Persia through the ports of the west coast, and later from the Portuguese at Goa. That dependency shaped everything: foreign policy, the wars with the sultanates, the welcome given to Portuguese traders, the wealth that had to be raised to keep paying. Look at the horses carved on the Mahanavami platform and on the temple wall bands. They are not decoration. They are the most expensive thing the empire imported.
chunks.source_name: BA Notes, Paes and Nuniz on Vijayanagara

chunks.title: Two brothers, a sage, and a conversion
chunks.body: The founding story adds a figure the textbooks sometimes drop. Harihara and Bukka had been captured and taken north, and tradition says they converted to Islam there before returning south. The sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri is said to have received them back and set them to found a Hindu kingdom on the Tungabhadra. Whether the conversion happened is argued. What is certain is that the Sringeri monastery backed the new state, that its head was honoured in the capital, and that you can see Vidyaranya carried in procession painted on the ceiling of the Virupaksha hall.

chunks.title: Everything here was cut with iron and patience
chunks.body: There is no shortcut hiding in these temples. Every surface at Belur and Halebidu was cut by hand with iron tools, by men working under a patron who paid by the year rather than the piece. A single bracket figure with drilled chains and separate beads could take one carver months. The Hoysalas spent more than a century of continuous employment on two buildings. That is the real scale of what you are looking at, and it is a better number to carry around than any measurement of height or width. This is a hundred years of somebody's working life, in stone.

chunks.title: Ramanuja came here in exile
chunks.body: The philosopher Ramanuja fled south India persecution and spent years in the Hoysala country in the early twelfth century. Tradition holds that he cured the king's daughter, that Vishnuvardhana turned from Jainism to Vaishnavism under his influence, and that the Chennakeshava temple at Belur followed. Ramanuja went on to reshape the Srivaishnava tradition across the south, including at Srirangapatna and Melkote near Mysuru. So a dispute somewhere in Tamil country produced a refugee, and the refugee produced a king's conversion, and the conversion produced the building in front of you.
