chunks.title: A temple that was buried to save it
chunks.body: There is a pattern across this region that is worth knowing. When raids came down from the north in the fourteenth century, communities in several places buried images, walled up shrines and let temples be covered over rather than see them broken. Some were recovered centuries later, intact, when a farmer's plough or a road cutting found them. That is one reason the sculpture in the Halebidu museum is in better condition than the sculpture still on the temple wall. Protection here often meant burial. What survives best is what somebody hid.
chunks.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Karnataka recovery records, general reference

chunks.title: You are drinking a smuggled crop
chunks.body: Every cup of coffee poured in this district descends from a crime. Yemen controlled the coffee trade and exported only roasted beans so that nothing could be planted elsewhere. Baba Budan carried seven live beans out past the guards. That single act broke a monopoly and started an industry that now employs hundreds of thousands of people in these hills. Look at the plants under the shade trees as you drive. Genetically, a great many of the arabica plants in India trace back to a very narrow founding stock. It is a large industry standing on a very small beginning.

chunks.title: This district produced two army chiefs
chunks.body: Kodagu is one of the smallest districts in Karnataka and it has supplied a strikingly large share of the Indian Army's officers, including Field Marshal Cariappa, the first Indian commander-in-chief, and General Thimayya, who commanded during the 1962 war. Both were Kodavas from here. You will see their names on schools, roads and memorials all over Madikeri. Ask why and you will get answers about martial tradition, about land tenure that kept families on the same estates, and about a community small enough that everybody's service is known. All three are part of it.

chunks.title: The British called it Coorg and took it in a fortnight
chunks.body: Kodagu was an independent kingdom until 1834. The last raja, Chikka Virarajendra, fell out with the East India Company, and a British force came over the ghats and took the country in a campaign of about two weeks. He was deposed and exiled, eventually to Benares, and later travelled to England to press his case. His daughter Gowramma was taken to Britain, baptised with Queen Victoria as godmother, and died young. The kingdom that resisted Tipu Sultan for decades was finished by a fortnight's campaign and then absorbed into a district.

chunks.title: The rain here arrives as a wall
chunks.body: If you are in Kodagu in June or July, stand outside and wait. The monsoon does not drizzle in. It comes over the ridge as a grey wall you can watch approaching across the valley, and then it is on you and you cannot hear anyone speak. Parts of this district take several thousand millimetres a season. That water is what makes the coffee, the pepper and the Kaveri. It also cuts the roads and moves hillsides. People here plan their year around it rather than complaining about it. Stand under a tiled verandah and listen to it for ten minutes.

chunks.title: A goddess who was a wife first
chunks.body: The story of the Kaveri told here is not about geography. Kaveri was married to the sage Agastya on one condition: he must never leave her alone. He did, setting her down in his water pot while he went to bathe. She took it as release, turned to water and flowed away down the hill. His disciples tried to stop her and she went underground and came up further on. That is why the river vanishes and reappears along its upper course. The tank at Talakaveri is where she left. Kodavas honour her as an ancestor, not only as a river.

chunks.title: Hockey, and a tournament of families
chunks.body: Kodagu plays hockey the way some places play cricket. Every year one family hosts the Kodava Hockey Namme, a tournament in which teams enter by family name, and it has run to hundreds of entries in a single edition, making it one of the largest field hockey tournaments anywhere. The host family changes each year and the whole district turns up. If you are here in the spring, ask where it is being held. It is not a tourist event and nobody is selling tickets, which is exactly why it is worth an afternoon.
chunks.source_name: Kodava Hockey Namme records, general reference

chunks.title: The pensioners' town became the software capital
chunks.body: Within living memory this was known as a place people retired to: cool, green, slow, full of gardens and government offices. Then in 1985 Texas Instruments opened a design centre here, followed by Infosys and Wipro and a satellite link that let engineers work directly with clients abroad. Within two decades the population more than doubled. Almost nobody planned for it. The roads, the water supply and the lakes are all still catching up with a change that happened in one generation. When someone here complains about traffic, they are describing that arithmetic.

chunks.title: A tree survey, and a man who counted them
chunks.body: Bengaluru's tree cover is not accidental. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the Mysore state horticulture department, under superintendents including Gustav Krumbiegel, planted avenues across the city and chose species so that different streets flowered in different months. That is why in March one road turns pink with tabebuia and in April another goes yellow, and in May the gulmohar comes. Krumbiegel is buried here. Walk any old cantonment street and look up. Somebody chose that tree, for that road, over a hundred years ago, and wrote down why.
chunks.source_name: Horticulture Department, Government of Karnataka, general reference

chunks.title: Winston Churchill may still owe the club money
chunks.body: Churchill was posted to Bangalore as a young cavalry officer in 1896 and lived in the cantonment. The Bangalore Club keeps a ledger with an unpaid bill in his name for a sum of a few rupees, and they have never written it off. It is on display. The story is worth more than the money. It is a reminder that this half of the city was a British garrison town for a century and a half, with its own clubs, churches, parade grounds and street names, and that the people of the pete a few kilometres west lived under an entirely different administration.

chunks.title: A plague reshaped the map
chunks.body: In 1898 plague came to Bangalore and killed thousands. The response reshaped the city. New extensions were laid out on open ground away from the crowded pete, with wide streets, water supply and drainage: Basavanagudi and Malleshwaram, both planned in the years after the outbreak. If you have wondered why those two neighbourhoods have straight numbered cross streets and the old town does not, that is the reason. A public health emergency drew the grid. The Bull Temple was already there. The suburb was laid out around it. Walk a numbered cross street and you are walking the public health response.

chunks.title: The city where a dosa has a queue at seven
chunks.body: Start here rather than at a monument. Bengaluru's real institution is the darshini: a small stand-up eating house, no table service, pay first at the counter, food in three minutes. There are thousands of them and they are how the city eats. The oldest ones have queues on the pavement before seven in the morning. Order idli vada, or a masala dosa, and a filter coffee. Eat standing. It costs less than a bus ticket in most cities and it is better than most restaurant food you will pay ten times for here.
